measurement.happened:
The single dominant story of the week was the unprecedented trilateral summit between Trump, Xi, and Putin in China, which drew headlines from every source. Trump arrived in China, was given a rare airport welcome by Xi, and the three leaders met in what multiple outlets called a 'new Yalta.' They issued a joint 'peace declaration' on nuclear risks, but analysts noted it was more symbolic than substantive, with no real breakthroughs on arms control. Trump called Putin 'my friend' and shook his hand on camera, which drew immediate backlash from Zelensky, who called Putin a 'killer.' Russia framed the meeting as a watershed moment and a snub to Europe, while China's Xi quietly strengthened his own hand. The summit's aftermath spilled into domestic politics, with Trump defending his 'fantastic' ties to both leaders while facing what AFP called 'tumult at home.' Trump also floated the idea of his chief of staff running for president in 2028, and Elon Musk publicly distanced himself, saying 'I am not MAGA' and calling his record $446 million midterm spending 'pretty foolish.'

The second major theme was the midterm election results and the reshaping of Congress. Democrats flipped nine US Senate seats, the most in nearly seventy years, and secured fifty-six Senate seats, their broadest majority in sixteen years. Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate seat, a rare bright spot for Democrats. In the House, Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker, who would become the first Black Speaker in US history. Reuters noted that the most new Black Democrats in decades would join Congress and were set to sway policy. Trump, however, insisted Alaska voters 'chose the wrong Dan Sullivan,' and the Justice Department dropped its appeal in the Alaska Senate suit. The new Democratic leadership immediately began organizing: a new leader pledged to target Trump corruption, Democrats opened a probe into Nvidia's influence on the Megaspeed investigation, and they sent letters to dozens of Trump officials putting them on notice. Sen. Tim Kaine said he would force votes on the human rights consequences of US policies in Russia.

The third major theme was the ongoing Iran war and Gulf tensions. The US struck Iran's Qeshm island after an attack on a US base in Bahrain, and Iran widened its Gulf attacks in response. Kuwait reported repelling its first Iranian attack in two months. Iran said it downed US drones over the Strait of Hormuz, and the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian 'trustees' collecting oil revenues. The US military returned two aircraft carriers to the Middle East. In Congress, Republicans blocked an Iran war resolution, and lawmakers were divided over the conflict. Trump said he wanted a 'permanent' deal to stop Iran getting nuclear weapons but called Iran's terms 'unacceptable.' Vice President Vance declined to say he would have ordered the strikes. The US also sanctioned Singapore and Malaysia on Iran compliance, and a Pakistani man was sentenced to twenty-seven years for a foiled Iran-backed plot to kill Trump and Biden.

The fourth theme was the Nvidia and AI technology storm. The SEC opened an investigation into Nvidia's accounting, and former CEO Jensen Huang agreed to testify at a public Senate hearing. Trump urged Huang to apologize and called for his reinstatement, calling him 'brilliant.' The AI tech rout prompted investors to rush into value stocks, and US AI chip curbs hit Chinese tech stocks, spurring a self-sufficiency push. Trump announced the US would penalize firms building data centers abroad, and the FCC granted tech import waivers. Anthropic's IPO price hit $83 per share on strong demand. Meanwhile, Waymo pulled all its self-driving cars from US freeways after a California ban, and the US confirmed it was probing Megaspeed over chip exports.

The fifth theme was a wave of cyber and security breaches. Hackers breached the Department of Agriculture, and the FBI's crime database was also hit. Most alarmingly, the highly classified NSA national security communications network went offline, confirmed by multiple sources. Security officials said 'malicious' activity was not behind the broader US tech outages, but the incidents rattled the government. Trump downplayed the FBI breach while reviving complaints about the agency's Russia probe, and said there could be a 'positive spin' from the hack. The US Transportation Department watchdog launched an audit of FAA oversight of Boeing, and US flights were nearly back to normal after a rare no-takeoff order.

The sixth theme was the measles outbreak. The US officially lost its measles elimination status after twenty-six years, with cases approaching six thousand and the outbreak worsening. Doctors called it 'a ghost from the past.' The US and Mexico both lost measles-free status. This became a significant public health story alongside the approval of a $7.25 billion Roundup cancer settlement by a US judge.

The seventh theme was the Trump administration's internal and legal battles. A second judge blocked Trump's triumphal arch in Washington, calling it a 'rushed job,' and a judge issued a fourteen-day extension of the order blocking it. A judge rejected the administration's homelessness program revamp, and another questioned its refugee policies. A judge ordered the agriculture secretary to stop sending religious emails from an official account, calling them unconstitutional. The House was found to have unconstitutionally passed a spending bill in 2022. Trump ordered federal contractors to check with the White House before responding to Congress, a move seen as an assertion of executive power. The Navy decided not to rename a carrier to honor a Black war hero after considering switching it to Trump's name.

The eighth theme was trade and the economy. Trump touted his Asia trade deal wins, but US agricultural exports disappointed. The US challenged Airbus's three billion euro EIB financing, raising fears of renewed transatlantic trade tensions. Traders began moving US copper to China as tariff fears eased. US car dealerships reported being low on EV models. Mortgage rates rose to 7.28 percent, ending a four-week slide. A tentative deal averted a strike threat at the busiest US ports. US equity funds drew inflows for a third straight week, and strong retail sales pointed to a happy holiday season. The Senate passed a bipartisan bill to speed energy and infrastructure projects.

The ninth theme was military and defense moves. Defense Secretary Hegseth restricted military ties with Canada, and the Pentagon signed a military cooperation deal in Venezuela after Maduro's ouster. The US Army delayed the detonation of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa after public safety concerns. The US backed Colombia's plans to resume aerial coca spraying. Denmark ratified a security deal providing the US expanded military access in Greenland. The US floated the idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, and Russia pushed back against US ideas of NATO-style security guarantees.

The tenth theme was immigration and the border. A migrant caravan in Mexico began walking toward the US border. US deportees in South Sudan reportedly went hungry as guards pocketed money from relatives. The appeals court halted an order restoring Venezuelan TPS. A former Venezuelan boxer was detained by US immigration and faced deportation. A Honduran court acquitted two US citizens of trafficking charges in the Angie Pena case.

Smaller but notable stories included: Trump's posthumous pardon of baseball legend Pete Rose, the US losing measles-free status, Voyager 1 reaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a Florida pastor convicted in the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Moise, an Irish man charged with destroying a US military C-130 aircraft with an axe, a Russian arrested for spying on Palantir, the US confirming a probe into Megaspeed, and the US officially losing measles elimination status. Trump also praised the Philippine alliance during his Manila visit, and the US signed a military deal with Venezuela less than a year after Maduro's removal.
measurement.expected:
The most immediate story will be the domestic political fallout from the midterm results and the trilateral summit. With Democrats holding fifty-six Senate seats and Hakeem Jeffries set to become Speaker, expect a wave of committee assignments, oversight announcements, and early legislative moves in the first few days of the new Congress. The Democrats' pledge to target Trump corruption, their Nvidia/Megaspeed probe, and Kaine's human rights votes will likely generate headlines. Trump, meanwhile, will face pressure to reconcile his 'friend' rhetoric about Putin and Xi with the new Democratic majority that is openly critical of the summit. Expect a near-certain clash between the White House and the new congressional leadership over the Iran war authorization, the budget, and executive orders. The government shutdown risk remains live, as Congress struggled this week to avert one and the new Democratic Senate will be less willing to rubber-stamp spending. I rate a shutdown or a short funding extension as probable within the next seven days.

The Iran war will continue to dominate foreign policy. With two US carriers back in the Middle East, Iran downing drones over Hormuz, and Gulf states under attack, the risk of further escalatory strikes is high. Trump's stated desire for a 'permanent' nuclear deal will clash with his 'unacceptable' framing of Iran's terms. I expect at least one more round of US strikes or Iranian retaliatory attacks in the Gulf, possibly involving shipping lanes. The Senate's blocked war resolution means the executive retains broad latitude, but the new Democratic majority may push for another vote. I rate further Gulf combat as probable, a negotiated pause as possible, and a full all-out war as unlikely but not impossible.

The Nvidia and Jensen Huang story will keep generating headlines. Huang's Senate testimony is set, the SEC investigation is active, and Democrats have opened their own probe. Trump's public call for Huang's reinstatement and his urging Huang to apologize create a strange dynamic. I expect the Senate hearing to be scheduled within the next week or the following, and I rate a significant political drama around the hearing as probable. The AI chip curbs and their impact on China will continue to play out, with Chinese firms accelerating self-sufficiency efforts. The broader AI tech rout in markets may stabilize or deepen, but a full-blown tech correction is possible.

The measles outbreak will continue to worsen, with cases likely climbing past six thousand. Expect more states to report clusters, public health officials to issue warnings, and the political fight over vaccination mandates or school attendance policies to intensify. The loss of elimination status will be a talking point in the new Congress. I rate continued case growth as almost certain, a federal emergency declaration as possible, and a major political crisis over the outbreak as unlikely.

The cyber breaches will keep reverberating. The NSA network outage, the USDA hack, and the FBI database breach will fuel congressional oversight demands, especially from the new Democratic majority. Expect hearings, requests for classified briefings, and possibly a new cybersecurity executive order or legislative proposal. The 'malicious activity' question will remain unresolved, and I rate a follow-up breach or a government report as probable. Trump's attempt to find a 'positive spin' will likely be met with skepticism.

The triumphal arch legal battle will continue. With a second judge blocking it and a fourteen-day extension in place, the next court date will likely fall within the coming week. I expect either a further stay, a partial ruling, or the administration appealing to the Supreme Court. The families of the fallen at Arlington will keep the emotional stakes high. I rate a continued legal stalemate as probable and a definitive resolution as unlikely within seven days.

The migrant caravan walking toward the US border will reach the border region within the next few days. Expect a border enforcement response, possibly a new executive order on processing, and political theater from both parties. The new Democratic Congress will use it to pressure the administration on immigration policy. I rate a visible border standoff as probable, a major policy shift as possible, and a full border crisis as unlikely.

On the economy, the tentative port deal averts an immediate strike, but the mortgage rate rise to 7.28 percent and the AI tech rout will keep markets volatile. The Senate's energy and infrastructure bill will move to the House, where the new Democratic majority may reshape it. I expect continued equity fund inflows but growing caution, and the holiday retail season will be a key data point. A full market correction is possible but not the base case.

Less likely surprises: a sudden US-Iran ceasefire announced from behind the scenes (possible but not the base case); a major new cyber breach revealing the NSA network was targeted by a specific foreign actor (possible); Trump announcing a major cabinet reshuffle or a surprise pardon beyond Pete Rose (possible); a second judge or the Supreme Court taking up the triumphal arch case within the week (unlikely); a major natural disaster or hurricane hitting the US coast (unlikely in late November but not impossible); the Alaska Senate race triggering a recount or legal challenge that delays the new majority (unlikely).

Things I would not bet on: a full US-Iran ground war within seven days; a US government shutdown lasting more than a few days; a US recession declaration or a major banking crisis; a second impeachment inquiry against Trump before the new Congress even organizes; a US presidential succession crisis; a major US trade war with the EU triggered by the Airbus financing challenge; a US entry into a NATO-style security guarantee for Ukraine; a second US presidential election or a constitutional crisis over the 2022 spending bill ruling.

A week ago it was a scheduled event on the calendar, something the White House and Kremlin had confirmed and the press was previewing. By the second photograph it has become the single dominant story, the event around which everything else orbits. Trump got a rare airport welcome from Xi, the three leaders shook hands, issued a joint peace declaration on nuclear risks, and the world immediately called it a new Yalta. The summit grew from a diplomatic appointment into a defining moment, and its aftermath spilled into domestic politics, with Trump defending his friendship with Putin while facing what AFP called tumult at home. Elon Musk, who was supposed to be a quiet sidekick on the trip, instead publicly said he is not MAGA and called his record forty-four-sixty million dollar midterm spending pretty foolish, which is a new wrinkle that was not present in the first photograph.

The midterm election story also grew substantially. In the first photograph, the results had just come in: Democrats swept several races, MAGA influencers were reeling, and the political fallout was fresh. By the second photograph, the full scope is visible. Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most in nearly seventy years, and secured fifty-six seats. Hakeem Jeffries was nominated as Speaker and would become the first Black Speaker in US history. The new leadership immediately went on offense: opening a probe into Nvidia's influence, sending letters to dozens of Trump officials, and pledging to target what they call corruption under the administration. The story moved from election night shock to institutional reshaping.

Iran grew from a tense but de-escalating situation into an active war. In the first photograph, Trump was telling advisers he might hold off on strikes, Rubio was saying more military action was not needed, and the overall tone was cautious pause. By the second photograph, the US had struck Iran's Qeshm island after an attack on a US base in Bahrain, Iran had widened its Gulf attacks, Kuwait had repelled its first Iranian strike in two months, the US had returned two aircraft carriers to the Middle East, and Congress was divided over the conflict. This is the single biggest theme that expanded in intensity between the two photographs.

The Nvidia and AI story grew in institutional weight. A week ago it was a scandal with questions about Alice Huang and a probe into chip smuggling. By the second photograph, the SEC had opened a formal accounting investigation, Jensen Huang had agreed to testify at a public Senate hearing, Trump had urged Huang to apologize and called for his reinstatement, the AI tech rout had spooked investors into value stocks, and the US was probing Megaspeed over chip exports. The story moved from a personal and corporate scandal into a structural fight over America's AI supremacy.

A new and major theme appeared in the second photograph: a wave of cyber and security breaches. The NSA's national security communications network went offline, hackers breached the Department of Agriculture, and the FBI's crime database was hit. None of this was present in the first photograph, where security stories were about an Army spy in the UK, a Binance crypto seizure, and Guatemalan gangs. The second photograph shows a much broader and more alarming picture of digital vulnerability across the US government.

The Trump administration's legal and internal battles grew in volume. In the first photograph, the main legal story was Trump aiming to cut judicial power and the Kennedy family's arch challenge. By the second photograph, a second judge had blocked the arch, a judge rejected the homelessness program revamp, another questioned refugee policies, a judge ordered the agriculture secretary to stop sending religious emails, the House was found to have unconstitutionally passed a spending bill in 2022, and the Navy decided not to rename a carrier after a Black war hero. The pattern of courts and internal institutions pushing back on the administration accelerated.

The air traffic ground stop, which was the defining domestic story in the first photograph, shrank dramatically. By the second photograph, flights were nearly back to normal, and the story had been reduced to a mention of a rare no-takeoff order and a Transportation Department audit of FAA oversight of Boeing. The copper wiring and L3 Harris saga, the fifty billion dollar modernization request, the stranded passengers, the sports travel chaos: all of it faded from the headline position into the background.

The New York building collapse, the Washington DC fitness center shooting, the SS United States being deliberately sunk, the SoftBank data center writedown, the Uber data breach, the BMW fire-risk recall, the Guatemalan gang terrorist designations, the Army spy in the UK, the Binance crypto seizure, the Ozempic and Zepbound eye warnings: all of these stories from the first photograph have largely vanished from the second. They were absorbed into the noise or simply gave way to bigger stories.

The measles outbreak grew from a status update to a defining public health event. In the first photograph, the US had lost its measles-free status and the CDC chief said the agency would not change its response. By the second photograph, cases had approached six thousand, the outbreak was worsening, doctors called it a ghost from the past, and both the US and Mexico had lost elimination status. The story became more urgent and more concrete.

The migrant caravan grew from a group that had left Tapachula with the note that it was not heading to the US immediately, to a group actively walking toward the US border. The border story also gained new dimensions: deportees in South Sudan going hungry, a Venezuelan boxer detained, the Angie Pena case acquittal in Honduras, and an appeals court halting the Venezuelan TPS restoration.

New stories that appeared in the second photograph with no counterpart in the first include: the Waymo self-driving car pullout after a California ban, Anthropic's IPO at eighty-three dollars per share, the Airbus EIB financing challenge, the Denmark-Greenland security deal, the Iowa bomb-making chemical detonation delay, the Colombia coca spraying resumption, the Navy carrier naming dispute, Trump's posthumous pardon of Pete Rose, the Roundup cancer settlement approval, the Pakistani man sentenced for the Iran-backed Trump and Biden assassination plot, the Voyager one light-day milestone, the Florida pastor conviction in the Moise assassination, the Irish man who destroyed a C-130 with an axe, the Russian arrested for spying on Palantir, and the House spending bill being found unconstitutional. These are the fresh arrivals in the second photograph.

What this says about the way expectations have been wrong for this country: the pattern is that the expectations tend to be right about the broad direction of institutional and political stories (Congress, courts, trade) but consistently underestimate the speed and intensity of military escalation (Iran), overestimate the staying power of single-incident stories (building collapse, air traffic), and underweight the potential for sudden cyber and security shocks that can appear out of nowhere and dominate the news cycle. The country's news cycle in this period is driven less by a single narrative arc and more by a constant churn of institutional friction, where courts, Congress, the military, and the tech sector all push back on the administration simultaneously, and the expectations struggle to capture that multidirectional pressure.
delta.driver: The force pushing the United States from the first photograph to the second is the collision of three simultaneous repositionings that are all happening at once and feeding off each other. First, the country is repositioning itself in the global order: the Shenzhen summit with Xi and Putin is a deliberate attempt to reset the three-power balance, and the military moves in the Gulf, the Venezuela deal, the Denmark-Greenland agreement, and the Colombia coca spraying are all pieces of a broader assertion of American reach and partnership. Second, the country is repositioning its internal power structure: the Democratic sweep of nine Senate seats and the installation of Jeffries as Speaker is not just a change in voting arithmetic but a fundamental shift in who controls the levers of oversight, budget, and investigation, and the new Congress is immediately going on offense against the administration in ways that the first photograph could only preview. Third, the country is repositioning its relationship with technology and security: the Nvidia-SEC investigation, the AI chip curbs, the NSA network going offline, the USDA and FBI breaches, and the Waymo pullout all point to a moment where the digital infrastructure that the country has been building for decades is simultaneously a source of national advantage and a source of vulnerability, and the administration is being forced to manage both at the same time. Underneath all three of these repositionings is a constant tension between the executive branch's appetite for unilateral action and the institutional counterweights of courts, Congress, and the media, a tension that is producing a higher volume of legal challenges, congressional probes, and public disputes in the second photograph than in the first. The speed at which these threads are tightening is what makes the week feel so compressed: the summit, the Congress, the war, the cyber breaches, the measles outbreak, and the AI rivalry are all accelerating in the same seven days, and the country is being pulled in several directions at once by forces that are not fully under anyone's control.

The corruption letters will generate at least one public response from a Trump official. A formal impeachment inquiry or censure resolution is possible but not yet certain. The less likely surprise: a unified Democratic-Republican bill on energy or infrastructure passing quickly, as the Senate already passed a bipartisan energy bill this week, setting a precedent for early cooperation.

Theme 3: Nvidia, AI, and the tech-security complex. Direction: institutional escalation continues. Confidence: high that the Senate testimony happens and generates fallout, medium on the specific revelations. Huang will testify, the SEC investigation will produce more filings, the Megaspeed probe will widen. The NSA network being offline, USDA and FBI hit, will generate CISA briefings to Congress, possibly a classified session. The administration will either identify the actor or offer a plausible denial. A political fight over IT modernization funding is likely. The less likely surprise: a second major federal system breach being revealed as the first investigations deepen, which the motion makes more probable than it looks because the pattern of multiple simultaneous hits suggests a coordinated campaign rather than isolated incidents.

Theme 5: Measles and public health. Direction: worsening, with more state-level action. Confidence: high. Cases will continue to climb past 6,000. More schools will close. A CDC press conference is likely. The political fight over vaccine mandates and funding will intensify. The US-Mexico shared loss of elimination status will be a talking point. This will not be the top story but will be a persistent undercurrent.

Theme 6: Summit aftermath and domestic diplomacy. Direction: continued friction between the White House's diplomatic record and the new Congress's scrutiny. Confidence: medium. The 'new Yalta' framing will be used by Democrats to question the administration's nuclear posture. Zelensky's 'killer' comment will resurface in hearings. Musk's 'I am not MAGA' distancing will be a sidebar. Trump's chief of staff as a 2028 candidate will generate speculation. The less likely surprise: a formal Congressional resolution questioning the legal authority of the trilateral peace declaration, which would be a significant institutional test.

Theme 7: Legal and judicial battles. Direction: continued pushback from the courts. Confidence: medium-high. At least one more ruling against the administration is likely. The spending bill's unconstitutionality may have budgetary implications. The arch case will continue. The refugee and homelessness policy challenges will generate more rulings. The less likely surprise: a judge blocking a new executive order or initiative that has not yet been announced, which the motion of multiple simultaneous challenges makes more probable.

Theme 8: Trade, economy, and markets. Direction: mixed, with continued policy friction. Confidence: medium. The Airbus EIB challenge will generate EU responses. Mortgage rates at 7.28 percent will keep housing soft. Holiday retail data will be strong. The port strike averted will be a positive. The Senate energy bill will be implemented. The less likely surprise: a new tariff announcement targeting a specific sector, which Trump's pattern of trade threats makes more probable than a quiet week.

Theme 9: Immigration and the border. Direction: the caravan reaches or approaches the border, triggering a political response. Confidence: medium-high. The caravan is walking toward the US. The South Sudan deportee story will generate humanitarian coverage. The Venezuelan TPS halt will be challenged in court. The less likely surprise: a new executive order on border enforcement or a temporary surge of agents at the border, which the administration's pattern of reactive moves makes probable.

Theme 10: Military and defense. Direction: continued repositioning of alliances and partnerships. Confidence: medium. The Canada military ties restriction will generate a Canadian response. The Venezuela deal will be implemented. The Denmark-Greenland deal will be discussed. The Navy carrier naming dispute will resurface. The less likely surprise: a new defense cooperation deal or a significant change in military posture in the Indo-Pacific, which the summit's three-power framing makes more probable.

crystal.tldr: Next week is likely to be defined by continued Iran strikes and a loud Congressional war-powers debate, the new Democratic Congress hitting the ground running with oversight probes and budget fights, and follow-up fallout from the NSA, USDA, and FBI cyber breaches. crystal.eli5:
Imagine the United States is like a big school where the principal (the president) just had a fancy meeting with two other school principals from far away, and everyone is still arguing about whether that meeting was a good idea. At the same time, a new group of student council leaders just got elected, and they are already marching into the principal's office with a list of things they want to investigate. And in the cafeteria, there is a food fight between two countries that keeps getting worse every day.

The biggest thing happening is the fight with Iran. The US hit an island, Iran hit back at ships and bases in the Gulf, and now two big US warships are sailing back to the area. Congress is arguing about whether the president can keep doing this without asking them first. It is not over, and it probably will not be over by next weekend. There might be another strike, or a ship might get hit, or someone might try to make a deal. Any of those things is possible.

The new group of lawmakers who just got elected are already in action. They want to look into a big computer chip company called Nvidia, they want to figure out if the president's people did anything shady, and they want to make rules about how the country spends its money. One of them, a man named Hakeem Jeffries, is going to be the leader of the bigger group of lawmakers, and he is the first person from a certain background to hold that job. They are moving fast, and the president's team is not happy about it.

There is also a whole mess with computers and security. The secret phone network that the top security people use went dark for a while. Two other big government computer systems got hacked. Nobody is 100 percent sure who did it or why, but it is making everyone nervous. Meanwhile, the chip company story is getting bigger, with a formal investigation and a big hearing where the CEO has to answer questions under oath. And there is a measles outbreak that is getting worse, with thousands of sick people and the country officially losing its 'we got rid of measles' status for the first time in 26 years.

So the next week is going to be loud. There will be more strikes in the Gulf, more arguments in Congress, more news about the computer hacks and the chip company, and more worries about measles. It is a lot happening all at once, and nobody in charge has a clean plan for how to make it all stop.

emoji_reasons: The Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit in China was the week's defining global event, reshaping alliances, provoking backlash from Europe and Ukraine, and setting the stage for a new diplomatic order.

Democrats flipped nine Senate seats and are set to install the first Black Speaker of the House, fundamentally altering the balance of power in Washington and setting up a new era of congressional oversight.

The US struck Iran's Qeshm island, Iran widened Gulf attacks, drones were downed over Hormuz, and two carriers returned to the region, making the Iran conflict the most active military front for the US this week.

measurement.happened:
THE TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT DOMINATES. The single biggest story of the week was the unprecedented trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. The three leaders issued a joint 'Declaration toward Peace,' shook hands on camera, and Putin carried his nuclear briefcase into the room. Trump called Putin 'my friend' and said they had a 'great relationship,' which infuriated Zelensky, who called Putin a 'killer' in response. The Kremlin framed the summit as a watershed moment and a deliberate snub to Europe, while European allies gathered in Berlin to coordinate a response. On substance, however, the summit produced no breakthroughs: Trump said nuclear arms limits with China and Russia would be 'very hard to achieve,' and the three-way nuclear rivalry the US now faces was described as unprecedented. Putin defended his 'Yalta' vision of a post-war order, and allies warned against a Yalta-style carve-up of Ukraine. The summit exposed what commentators called Europe's power deficit, as the big three met without European heads of state. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/18-11/20, AP 11/18-11/20, BBC 11/18-11/21, CNN 11/18-11/21, DW 11/17-11/18, FT 11/16-11/18, Bloomberg 11/18, Al Jazeera 11/16, WSJ 11/18.)

THE WAR OF BRIDGES ESCALATES. Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea multiple times this week, partially collapsing a section and what Zelensky called an 'unprecedented' attack. The bridge is crucial to Russia's war logistics and its assertion of control over Crimea. Ukraine used so-called 'flying modems' to help guide the strikes. Putin vowed a 'far more painful' response and ruled out a Black Sea or energy truce. Russia hit back at Kyiv's river crossings and other infrastructure. The cleanup of the damaged bridge section is expected to take months, according to Ukraine. The 'war of bridges' became a defining image of the week, with both sides targeting the other's most symbolic infrastructure. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19-11/20, AP 11/17-11/18, BBC 11/17-11/20, CNN 11/17, DW 11/18, FT 11/18, TV5Monde 11/17-11/18, WSJ 11/18, Bloomberg 11/17-11/21.)

RUSSIA UNLEASHES MASSIVE MISSILE AND DRONE BARRAGES ON UKRAINE. In direct retaliation for the bridge strikes and as a show of force before and after the summit, Russia launched some of its largest missile and drone attacks of the war. At least eight people were killed in one wave, a Russian 'triple-tap' attack killed a seven-year-old and an emergency worker in Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, and dozens more were reported dead or missing. Russia targeted energy facilities, transport infrastructure, and sea vessels. Zelensky called one of the strikes 'one of the largest.' The EU accused Russia of stalling peace talks specifically to hit power plants as winter approaches. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/20, AP 11/20, BBC 11/20-11/21, CNN 11/20-11/21, DW 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/21, TV5Monde 11/21.)

A RUSSIAN MISSILE LANDS IN POLAND. During NATO military exercises near the Polish border, a Russian missile struck Polish territory. Polish Prime Minister Tusk called it a likely 'intentional provocation.' NATO officially called it a violation of Polish airspace. This was the third Polish airspace violation in the period, and it happened while Europe was holding drills nearby, raising fears of a deliberate Russian test of European nerves. (Supporting headlines: AP 11/20, BBC 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/21, DW 11/21, TV5Monde 11/21, Reuters 11/20.)

THE BALTIC SEA AND NORTHERN EUROPE BECOME A HOTSPOT. A Russian cargo ship was hit by a drone in the Gulf of Finland, with the crew evacuating. Finland detected the attack. A Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace around the same time. Denmark announced it had thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a US-Ukrainian rapper on its soil, with two Danes suspected of being hired by Russian intelligence. Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat and pushed the EU to tighten travel curbs on Russians. Estonia announced it will close its land border with Russia on December 1, citing a foiled sabotage attempt on a drone factory, while Moscow decried a 'new Iron Curtain.' The Netherlands summoned the Russian ambassador after its Kyiv embassy was hit, and a mass leak of Deutsche Bank documents showed links to Russia and the Epstein case. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/20-11/21, AP 11/20, BBC 11/21, CNN 11/15, DW 11/16, FT 11/15, TV5Monde 11/16-11/21, WSJ 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/21, Bloomberg 11/16, CNBC 11/16.)

EUROPE TIGHTENS SANCTIONS AND PREPARES FOR TALKS. The EU sanctioned Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, and she stepped down days later. The EU proposed a 45-billion-euro loan to Ukraine borrowed against the EU budget. The EU plans a visa ban for former Russian combatants. Germany's Foreign Minister Wadephul said Berlin talks send a 'strong signal to Moscow.' Europe declared itself ready for talks with Russia on ending the war. Russia, however, pushed back against the US idea of NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine and said the EU's Kallas playing a role in talks would lead to their collapse. Kushner said Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like guarantees, and Russia grasped the US offer on European security to revive its own old demands. Putin proposed a second humanitarian ceasefire, which analysts questioned was a trap. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/16, 11/20-11/21, AP 11/20, BBC 11/20, CNN 11/20, DW 11/20, FT 11/15-11/16, Bloomberg 11/18, Al Jazeera 11/16, WSJ 11/15.)

RUSSIA'S ENERGY SECTOR UNDER STRAIN. Drone attacks nearly halved Russia's November oil refining capacity. More Russian regions limited fuel sales as refinery output dropped. Russia imported record volumes of petrol. Russia exported the most crude since July as drones hammered refineries. A Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil facility in Tatarstan. The Russian diesel deal under Trump struggled to reach the US market amid legal fears and criticism. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19-11/20, AP 11/18, FT 11/18, Bloomberg 11/17, WSJ 11/15, DW 11/17.)

DOMESTIC RUSSIAN STORIES. A Russian military transport plane crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 on board. A renowned Russian ornithologist was jailed over small donations to Navalny's anti-corruption foundation. A WSJ investigation exposed sex abuse as part of the system in a Russian POW camp. The IIHF website was hacked after Russia was barred from the World Junior Hockey tournament in Canada, and Putin publicly criticized the 'disregard' for the sports ruling. Russia appealed to the IOC. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/17-11/19, AP 11/17-11/19, BBC 11/17, CNN 11/17, DW 11/21, WSJ 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/16.)

RUSSIA REPOSITIONS ITSELF AS AN ASIAN POWER. At APEC, Putin declared Russia an 'integral part of Asia-Pacific.' He pitched Russia as a place to invest. Vietnam and Russia agreed to deepen energy cooperation. Russia and Georgia resumed direct dialogue with an official meeting in Minsk. Russian nuclear-capable bombers were spotted in Vietnam before departing. Two Russian military aircraft were reported near Taiwan, the second time in a week. Japan scrambled jets after suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19, AP 11/19, BBC 11/17, Bloomberg 11/18, Al Jazeera 11/16.)

ESPIONAGE AND INTELLIGENCE TENSIONS. The US Department of Justice charged a Russian national with targeting Palantir as a foreign agent. A US Army officer was taken into custody after being arrested in the UK for spying for Russia. The Netherlands summoned Russia's ambassador after its embassy in Kyiv was hit. A GPS signal loss in the Netherlands pointed to possible Russian sabotage. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19, AP 11/17-11/18, BBC 11/18, TV5Monde 11/16.)
measurement.expected:
THE SUMMIT AFTERMATH AND EUROPEAN REACTION. Almost certain: Europe will spend the coming week digesting the Trump-Xi-Putin summit and coordinating a unified response. The Berlin meeting of Ukraine's allies already happened, and we should expect follow-up statements, press conferences, and possibly a special EU or NATO meeting to address the 'peace declaration' and the security guarantees question. Russia will likely try to split Europe by offering bilateral talks while resisting multilateral frameworks. The Kallas dispute and the NATO-style guarantees debate will dominate. Probable: The EU's 45-billion-euro Ukraine loan proposal will face its first round of parliamentary debate or member-state consultations. Possible: Denmark and Estonia will push for a formal EU response to the Baltic Sea drone attack, the rapper assassination plot, and the border closure, potentially leading to a new round of targeted sanctions or travel restrictions on Russian citizens. Unlikely: A full EU-Russia formal negotiation track will be launched this week; the groundwork is being laid, but the architecture is not ready.

WAR OF BRIDGES AND RETALIATION CYCLE. Almost certain: Russia will continue to strike Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly energy and transport, as winter approaches and the EU has accused Moscow of timing attacks to hit power plants. Ukraine will likely continue targeting Russian logistics, including the damaged Crimea bridge and other bridges. Probable: The partially collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge will be a focal point of both propaganda and military planning. Russia will either rush a temporary repair or use the damage to justify a harder military posture in the Black Sea. Possible: A new round of drone swarms against Russian refineries, given that November refining is already nearly halved. Unlikely: A full-scale ground offensive by either side this week; the pattern is aerial and drone warfare, not tank pushes.

POLAND AND NORTHERN EUROPE TENSIONS. Almost certain: Poland will demand a formal explanation or apology from Russia over the missile that landed on its territory. NATO will issue a statement, and the three prior airspace violations will be cited as a pattern. Probable: Estonia's border closure on December 1 will take effect, and Russia will respond with a diplomatic note or a minor provocation near the border. Denmark will likely follow up the rapper plot with additional intelligence briefings to EU partners. Possible: Another Russian airspace incursion over the Baltic or over Poland, as Moscow appears to be testing European reaction thresholds. Unlikely: A full NATO Article 4 consultation or a formal Article 5 discussion this week; the incidents are serious but not yet at that threshold.

ENERGY AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE. Almost certain: Russian fuel shortages will worsen in several regions as refinery output stays depressed. More regions may impose fuel rationing or price controls. Probable: Russia will accelerate imports of refined petrol and diesel. The Russian diesel deal with the US will face further legal and political friction. Possible: Oil and gas prices will remain elevated, and the optical fiber price spike caused by drone-war damage to undersea cables will be felt in telecom costs. Unlikely: A major Russian budget revision or emergency economic package this week; the damage is accumulating but not yet at a crisis threshold.

DOMESTIC RUSSIA. Probable: The Siberian plane crash (19 dead) will generate a brief wave of domestic mourning and a state investigation, followed by the usual pattern of the story fading. The ornithologist's jailing over Navalny-foundation donations will be a small but symbolically charged case for opposition circles. The POW camp sex abuse story will generate some domestic and international outrage, but Russia will likely contain the narrative. Possible: The Wildberries CEO's departure will trigger a short internal reshuffle or a statement from the company's board. Unlikely: A major domestic political event, protest, or cabinet change this week. The regime is focused on the war and the post-summit diplomacy.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES. A Russian pre-emptive strike on a Ukrainian port or naval base in the Black Sea, citing the Baltic drone attack as justification. A sudden Russian offer of a full ceasefire or a major prisoner swap to mark the post-summit 'peace' mood. A second Polish or Baltic airspace incident within the same week, escalating the NATO response. A Russian cyberattack on a European energy grid or financial system in retaliation for the Wildberries sanctions. A dramatic statement from Putin at a domestic event (e.g., a Victory Day-style speech or a Duma address) reframing the war's goals.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON. A full-scale Russian ground offensive in a new sector. A major Russian nuclear test or a new ICBM launch for show. A Russian presidential election or succession announcement. A full EU-Russia trade deal or a lifting of any major sanctions. A Russian withdrawal from any occupied territory. A major Russian domestic protest or strike. A ceasefire that holds for more than 48 hours. A Russian space launch or satellite deployment as a signal. A major Russian budget deficit crisis or a rouble collapse.
emoji_reasons: The historic Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit in China, with its 'peace declaration' and the way it reshuffled global power dynamics, was the defining diplomatic event of the week.
Russia's massive retaliatory missile barrages on Ukraine, the repeated strikes on the Crimea bridge, and the missile landing in Poland made aerial and missile warfare the central military story.

The Russian cargo ship hit by a drone in the Gulf of Finland, the Danish rapper assassination plot, the Estonian border closure, and multiple Baltic and Nordic airspace violations turned the northern seas into a new flashpoint.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the dominant shift is from a week defined by diplomatic anticipation to one defined by diplomatic performance and military escalation in parallel. The Shenzhen summit, which in the first photograph was an announced future event, became in the second the single anchoring story, producing a joint 'Declaration toward Peace,' a photo op with Putin's nuclear briefcase in the room, and a visible snub to Europe. The theme that grew most dramatically was the 'war of bridges': Ukraine's repeated strikes on the Kerch Bridge, partially collapsing a section, and Russia's vow of a 'far more painful' response, turned infrastructure targeting into a symbolic and strategic contest that was not a named theme in the first photograph. Russian missile and drone barrages on Ukraine escalated from 'expected continuation' to some of the war's largest waves, including a triple-tap strike that killed a seven-year-old in Zelensky's hometown, which is a step up in both scale and human drama. The Baltic and Northern European front grew from scattered incidents (a warship hit, a data-center drone attack) into a coordinated hotspot: a cargo ship hit in the Gulf of Finland, a helicopter near Finnish airspace, a foiled assassination plot in Denmark, Estonia announcing it will close its land border on December 1, and a Russian missile landing in Polish territory during NATO exercises. This is a new cluster of events that was only hinted at in the first photograph. Russia's energy strain grew from 'refineries being hit' to 'November refining capacity nearly halved, record petrol imports, multiple regions rationing fuel,' which is a materially worse picture. Russia's Asian repositioning, which in the first photograph was an upcoming summit, became an explicit declaration: Putin calling Russia an 'integral part of Asia-Pacific,' nuclear-capable bombers spotted in Vietnam, and energy deals with Vietnam. The EU's role grew from internal squabbling over who to send to concrete actions: sanctioning Wildberries' CEO, proposing a 45-billion-euro loan to Ukraine, and a visa ban for former Russian combatants. What shrank or vanished: the prisoner exchange, expected to be a headline, is barely visible in the second photograph; the specific car-bombing narrative in Moscow fades; the bear population, the Madagascar story, the 'beer-loving nations alliance,' and the Novaya Gazeta closure are no longer active threads. The sports dispute did not shrink but intensified: Russia was formally barred from the World Junior Hockey tournament, the IIHF website was hacked, and Putin personally criticized the ruling. New domestic stories appeared: a military transport plane crash in Siberia killing 19, a WSJ investigation into sex abuse in a POW camp, and a renowned ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation. The espionage thread continued but shifted focus: a Russian national was charged by the US DOJ for targeting Palantir, and the UK Army officer case moved from arrest to formal custody. Overall, the motion is from anticipation and setup to performance and escalation: the diplomatic stage was set, the military stakes were raised, and the geographic footprint of the conflict widened northward and eastward.
delta.wind: The expectation that the Shenzhen summit would happen, produce a joint statement, and be more about positioning than substance was broadly correct. The summit happened, produced the 'Declaration toward Peace,' and Trump himself said nuclear arms limits would be 'very hard to achieve,' confirming the positioning-over-substance read. The Yalta comparisons materialized, and the European snub was exactly as predicted. The one miss was the prisoner exchange, which was expected to be a probable headline event between November 15 and 21; it does not appear as a major story in the second photograph, suggesting it either happened quietly, slipped, or was overshadowed by the summit and the bridge strikes. The expectation of continued drone strikes on Russian infrastructure was correct, but the form was different: the strikes were not just on refineries and ports but concentrated on the Kerch Bridge, creating a new 'war of bridges' theme that was not in the forecast. The expectation of 'probable that at least one major Russian refinery or port is hit again' was met, but the bridge was a more symbolic and strategically significant target than was anticipated. The EU sanctions package was expected to be adopted on November 17, and while the adoption itself is not the headline in the second photograph, the EU's subsequent actions (sanctioning Wildberries' CEO, the 45-billion-euro loan, the visa ban) show the sanctions track continued and evolved, which is consistent with the expectation but more specific than predicted. The expectation that Europe would finalize its delegation was partly met: the EU declared itself ready for talks, but the Kallas question became a point of contention rather than a clean resolution, and Russia said Kallas's involvement would lead to collapse. The expectation of 'possible one more targeted incident' domestically was met in a different form: the military transport plane crash in Siberia is more of an accident than a targeted strike, but it fits the pattern of domestic incidents. The oil and diesel expectation of 'continued volatility' was an understatement: the halving of November refining capacity and record petrol imports are a more severe deterioration than 'volatility' implies. The sports dispute expectation of 'probable the dispute continues' was correct but understated: the formal barring from the World Juniors, the website hack, and Putin's personal criticism pushed the dispute to a more heated level. The nuclear arms expectation of 'probable a statement, possible a framework, unlikely a signed treaty' was accurate: the joint declaration exists, no framework or treaty was signed, and Trump's 'very hard to achieve' remark confirms the gap. What was not expected and came: the Poland missile incident (listed as a less-likely surprise, but a missile in Polish territory during NATO exercises is more dramatic than a cyberattack on infrastructure); the Denmark assassination plot and Estonia border closure, which together form a new Baltic escalation cluster; the 'triple-tap' attack and the killing of a seven-year-old, which raised the human stakes beyond the 'dozens dead or missing' that was implied; Russia's explicit 'integral part of Asia-Pacific' declaration and the bombers in Vietnam, which made the Asian pivot from a sub-plot to a declared strategy; the 45-billion-euro EU loan and the visa ban for former combatants, which are concrete EU measures that go beyond the sanctions package that was forecast; and the WSJ POW camp investigation, which is a new domestic accountability story. What this says about the way expectations have been wrong for Russia: the forecast was structurally sound on the diplomatic track but underweighted the military escalation and the geographic widening of the conflict. The expectation treated the summit as the anchor and everything else as supporting cast, but in reality the bridge strikes and the Baltic incidents were co-equal stories. The expectation was too optimistic about the prisoner exchange being a visible headline and too conservative about the energy damage (halving of refining capacity is a step beyond 'volatility'). The expectation also underweighted Russia's deliberate Asian repositioning as a stated policy rather than a tactical move, and it did not anticipate the specific form of European coordination (Berlin meeting, loan, visa ban) that emerged as a package. The overall pattern is that the expectations captured the right themes but the wrong intensity and the wrong specific targets, and they treated the diplomatic and military tracks as sequential (summit first, then military) when in reality they ran in parallel and fed each other.
delta.driver: The force pushing Russia from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a great-power diplomatic performance and a war that is simultaneously intensifying and widening geographically. Russia is using the Shenzhen summit to lock in its status as one of three co-equal powers, to signal to Europe that the big decisions are being made without them, and to anchor its pivot toward Asia as a declared strategic direction rather than a fallback. At the same time, the military campaign is escalating in both intensity and symbolism: the Kerch Bridge strikes represent a new phase in which both sides target not just capacity but the physical and psychological links that hold territories together, and the triple-tap barrage in Kryvyi Rih is a message that the war is still very much a war of attrition with human cost. The Baltic and Polish incidents show that the shadow war is no longer a sub-plot but a parallel front, with Russia testing European nerves through airspace violations, sabotage plots, and a missile in Polish territory during NATO exercises, all of which raise the question of whether a miscalculation could become a trigger. Domestically, the halving of refining capacity, record fuel imports, and the transport plane crash are creating a pressure to either accelerate the diplomatic track or absorb the cost of a longer war. The underlying driver is therefore a three-way tension: Russia wants to be seen as a great power negotiating from strength, it needs to keep military pressure high enough to hold its leverage in the talks, and it must manage the domestic and economic costs of a war that is increasingly hitting its own soil, its own fuel supply, and its own symbolic infrastructure. The Asian pivot is the long-term hedge, the bridge war is the short-term lever, and the Baltic incidents are the pressure test for whether Europe will stay at the table or be pushed to the sidelines.

Some regions are already rationing, and people are probably going to start noticing longer lines at gas stations and higher prices. It's like a car where the gas tank is leaking and you're trying to drive to a really important meeting. The diplomatic meeting is the shiny part, but the leaking tank is the part that's going to hurt in the long run.

measurement.happened:
THE TRILATERAL SUMMIT IN SHENZHEN DOMINATES THE WEEK. The single biggest story is the historic three-way meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. China hosted the event and used it as a stage to project Xi as the indispensable architect of global order. The three leaders issued a joint 'Declaration toward Peace,' shook hands, hugged, and posed for what the Financial Times called a 'Yalta 2.0' moment. Chinese state media (TV5Monde's French coverage confirms this) erected Xi as the central figure who orchestrated the encounter. Trump arrived on the 18th, Putin landed the same day, and the trilateral talks took place on the 19th. Xi told the US to do the 'right thing' on Taiwan, praised a 'comprehensive turnaround' in China-Australia ties, and called for removing trade and investment barriers. Trump called the nuclear arms situation with China 'very hard' to resolve and said China's nuclear buildup was 'hot and heavy.' The diplomatic choreography was carefully managed: China barred a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral after she shouted a question, showed off Shenzhen's driverless taxis and robots to impress the visitors, and used airport greeting protocols to signal its relative ranking of each guest. Japan's PM Takaichi was notably made to look irrelevant by the optics, and 93 percent of Japanese now view China ties negatively. Canada's PM Carney used the summit to lock in further tariff cuts with China, hedging against US trade pressure. The summit was high on spectacle but thin on concrete deliverables, as multiple outlets noted. Headlines supporting this: virtually every source covered it; Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, AFP, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera all ran multiple stories.

THE NVIDIA AND AI CHIP CRISIS. The second major theme is the fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal and its impact on US-China chip relations. California's Attorney General subpoenaed Nvidia over concerns about its former CEO and China ties. The US signed off on nearly 900,000 AI chip sales to China in six months, but Nvidia stopped shipping Hopper chips to China. TSMC tightened curbs as new US rules closed a manufacturing loophole. The US moved to block China from indirect access to American AI technology, targeting Southeast Asian data centers. A bipartisan push in Congress gained momentum to ban or restrict Chinese car imports and tighten AI chip export rules. Blacklisted Chinese universities were found to have procured Nvidia chips. China's military was reported seeking advanced Nvidia chips for AI weapons. The Alice Huang probe (a former Nvidia executive) revealed her husband built a data-center empire backed by the Chinese state. A suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025. The scandal exposed a backdoor route that had kept Beijing in the AI race. China censored CNN's coverage of the Nvidia scandal. Singapore had to do damage control after the loophole was exposed. Headlines supporting this: Reuters, CNN, CNBC, WSJ, FT, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, BBC, AP, Deutsche Welle.

CHINA'S ECONOMIC SLOWDOWN AND MARKET SIGNALS. China's October economic data showed a deeper-than-expected slowdown: industrial output, retail sales, and investment all missed estimates. A Reuters poll sees home prices falling again in 2027. Copper hit its lowest since April amid AI market turmoil and Chinese demand concerns. China's $2 billion dollar bond in Hong Kong drew large orders but priced in line with US Treasuries, suggesting no premium for Chinese risk. China slashed its US Treasury holdings to a 2008 low. The offshore tax clampdown pushed China's budget into a rare surplus. China's top planner sought faster construction of state projects, signaling a stimulus push. China's export machine continued to shock the world, with solar cell exports rising for a second month on a tariff rush. Demand for Chinese goods was soaring but domestic economic momentum was slowing. China's Jetour planned $69 million Brazil car production investment. Headlines supporting this: Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera.

SOUTH CHINA SEA AND MARITIME TENSIONS. ASEAN and China fell short of agreeing on a code of conduct for the South China Sea. Analysts reported China was transforming a reef into a strategic forward outpost. Indonesia's President Prabowo and Xi discussed future South China Sea cooperation. Trump lauded the defense alliance with the Philippines ahead of China talks, signaling a US posture of checking Chinese maritime expansion. India and Japan deepened defense ties amid China and US uncertainty. Headlines supporting this: Al Jazeera, Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC, TV5Monde.

CHINA'S AI AND TECH SELF-SUFFICIENCY PUSH. China planned to strengthen AI token standards in its computing push. CCTV reported China expanding 5G across industries as 6G advances. Beijing's new strategy was described as 'Made by China, But Not Made in China.' Chinese robot makers in Shenzhen showed more than viral backflip videos. The US and allies signed an accord to protect AI supply chains from China. China's AI firms were described as 'addicted to Nvidia chips' and now facing withdrawal. SpaceX's subsidiary Cursor told lawmakers it was considering phasing out Chinese AI models. Headlines supporting this: Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Reuters, Al Jazeera.

OTHER NOTABLE ITEMS. Myanmar and China objected to a landmark ICJ ruling on the Rohingya genocide. China's defense minister made a surprise visit to Italy. The FDA rejected a cancer drug invented in China, a blow to Beijing's biotech sector. China's military banned SF Express from procurement over misconduct. K-pop giants positioned for a China return after a decade-long freeze. Chinese C-dramas and celebrities drew foreign fans. A massive boulder rolled down a mountain and slammed into a car. China's Mount Fuji warning (a family of a missing climber offered a reward). Rockstar promoted GTA VI in China despite lacking sales approval. China poached a top Harvard professor who now wants others to join. China flexed muscle in iron ore, squeezing Australia and its miners. China prepared to restart US private equity investments after a pullback. China's stand-up comedians entered their 'Rated R era.'

measurement.happened:
This week in DR Congo was dominated by two intertwined crises: a rapidly worsening Ebola outbreak and the ongoing military and diplomatic standoff with Rwanda over the M23 rebellion, all played out against the backdrop of the Francophonie summit in Cambodia.

THE EBOLA OUTBREAK (supported by nearly every source): The single biggest story of the week was the Ebola epidemic, now in its sixth month and clearly accelerating. The UN reported 5,500 deaths (Reuters, 11-18), while Deutsche Welle reported the caseload had just crossed 6,000 (11-21). Africa CDC declared the outbreak 'still not under control' (Reuters 11-16, Al Jazeera 11-15, AP 11-15). Reuters noted the virus is killing at a 'record pace' (11-17) and that scientists are still learning about this particular rare strain (11-20). Handicap International, cited by AFP (11-21) and TV5Monde (11-20), identified geography, ongoing violence, and community distrust as the three main obstacles to containment. Bloomberg (11-16) framed the crisis as being fueled by conflict and hunger, making it a compound emergency. The economic ripple effects were already visible: Barrick Gold furloughed some personnel at its Congo mines over Ebola concerns (Reuters, 11-17). A genuinely important development is that the WHO announced strain-specific Ebola vaccine trials are set to begin in DR Congo 'next week' (AFP, 11-17), which is a concrete near-term event. TV5Monde ran a video piece on the 'urgency' of containing the epidemic (11-16) and another on the 5,500+ dead (11-15).

RWANDA-DR CONGO TENSIONS AND M23 (supported by BBC, Al Jazeera, DW, TV5Monde, Reuters): The military conflict in the east, centered on the M23 rebel group, remained a major thread. BBC ran a dedicated M23 piece (11-18) and reported that the OIF (Operation of the Force, the regional military mechanism) is expected to come online within about two months (11-15). Al Jazeera reported that rival peace efforts have failed to halt violence in the east (11-18) and asked what is holding up the Washington-brokered peace process between Rwanda and DRC (11-18). Reuters noted that former Congo-based fighters are being retrained in Rwanda, swapping guns for new skills (11-20), suggesting both sides are preparing for a longer fight. DW described the M23 conflict as dividing the Francophone world (11-15). TV5Monde carried a video titled 'Humor as a weapon against war' (11-19), a small cultural note showing how the conflict permeates daily life.

THE FRANCOPHONIE SUMMIT (supported by AFP, DW, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera): The Francophone summit opened in Cambodia (11-15) and immediately became a stage for the DRC-Rwanda clash. AFP reported the summit 'opens with DR Congo, Rwandan clash' (11-15). DW noted Macron urged 'unity' and 'consensus' in the face of the tensions (11-15). TV5Monde ran multiple pieces on the summit and the DRC-Rwanda rift (11-15). DW also noted that DRC threatened to quit the Francophonie organization (11-15). Al Jazeera covered the summit opening amid the rift (11-15). This was a diplomatic flashpoint that amplified the bilateral conflict into a multilateral one.

US-DR CONGO MINERAL DEAL AND THE 'RESOURCES CURSE' (supported by BBC, TV5Monde, DW): BBC ran a feature asking whether a US-backed mineral highway can bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo (11-18). TV5Monde reported on the status of the bilateral US-DRC agreement on copper, cobalt, tin, and dams, now nearly a year after signing (11-18), and separately noted that US Democrats want to investigate Trump's mineral agreements in Africa, including with DRC, Zambia, and Kenya (11-19). DW published a piece on DRC's 'resources curse' (11-21), framing the country's vast mineral wealth as a source of both power and exploitation. This cluster of stories shows the mineral deal is a live political issue both in Kinshasa and in Washington.

SMALLER DOMESTIC NOTES (TV5Monde): Boat operators in wood went on strike (11-18). R&B star Héritier Wata announced he is 'already in the studio' with Fally Ipupa to record their long-awaited collaboration (11-18), a light cultural moment amid the crisis. These are minor but show the country's everyday life continuing.

DR Congo is dealing with a really bad Ebola outbreak that has been going on for about six months. More than 5,500 people have died, and the virus is a rare strain that scientists are still learning about. The big news for next week is that a new vaccine trial specifically for this strain is starting. That is a small step toward a cure, but the outbreak is not slowing down, and the places where it is hitting hardest are also where the war in the east is happening, which makes it harder to treat people and keep them safe.

At the same time, DR Congo and its neighbor Rwanda are still stuck in a tense standoff over a rebel group called M23. They are not at full-scale war right now, but they are both preparing for a longer fight. A regional peacekeeping force is supposed to start working in about two months, so next week is more about diplomacy and small skirmishes than a big battle. The two countries also got into a public argument at a French-language summit in Cambodia, and DR Congo even threatened to quit the whole organization, though that is more of a negotiating move than something that will actually happen next week.

A new thread that has been growing is the deal between the US and DR Congo about copper, cobalt, and other minerals. US politicians who are not in the president's party want to look into whether the deal is fair, and a big mining company already paused some work because of Ebola. So the health crisis, the war, and the money from minerals are all starting to tangle together in ways that make every story affect every other story. The government at home is trying to manage all of this, but the internal political fights from a few weeks ago have mostly quieted down because everyone is focused on the bigger emergencies.

measurement.happened:
This week in Iran was defined by an active, escalating war with the United States, punctuated by a brief diplomatic window that failed to produce results, and by a growing domestic crisis of energy and public confidence.

ACTIVE COMBAT AND ESCALATION: The central story is that the US-Iran war, which had been in a roughly two-month lull, reignited mid-week. On November 15, Iran struck a US military base in Bahrain with six drones, killing six US service members. On November 17, the US retaliated by striking an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran then widened its Gulf attacks, hitting targets in Kuwait and striking Bahrain a second time, with an industrial facility set on fire. A third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East on November 16. The US Navy chief admitted the war is straining maritime forces, and a whistleblower soldier filed a complaint over the deadly Iranian strike. The war's cost to the US has passed 48 billion dollars. Iran struck three tankers and showed off missile launchers on November 21. The US also hit key Iranian infrastructure, though it denied being behind tech outages. Trump said Iran is developing bioweapons and that the US is looking into a dirty-bomb plan. Iran threatened to strike civilian sites if the US does the same. (Headlines: Reuters 11-15, 11-16, 11-17, 11-18, 11-21; AP 11-17, 11-18; CNN 11-15, 11-17, 11-18; BBC 11-15, 11-18; FT 11-15, 11-17, 11-18; Al Jazeera 11-17, 11-18; TV5Monde 11-17, 11-18; Bloomberg 11-18, 11-19; WSJ 11-15, 11-17.)

DIRTY BOMB AND DC PLOT: A major intelligence story broke on November 16-17: US intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans to potentially detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, DC. Trump said the US takes it very seriously and that Iran would pay a major price if it carried it out. Secretary Rubio said there is no imminent threat to Washington. Iran dismissed the CNN report as propaganda. Trump also said Iran is looking at gas and bioweapons but downplayed the threat. This story dominated US political discussion for the rest of the week. (Headlines: CNN 11-16 through 11-18; Bloomberg 11-17; Al Jazeera 11-17; TV5Monde 11-17; BBC 11-17; CNBC 11-17; Reuters 11-17.)

HORMUZ AND MARITIME TENSION: The Strait of Hormuz was the economic battleground. Iran struck tankers, laid mines, and tightened its grip on shipping. The UK maritime agency reported two tanker incidents near Oman. Iran said a vessel hit a mine east of Hormuz. The US widened its blockade with curbs on oil transfers at sea, targeting ship-to-ship transfers. The UAE is shuttling oil past Iran in a risky operation. Oil prices fell for a third consecutive week as ample supply countered Iran risk, but the IEA warned the war could permanently slash reliance on Hormuz and that an energy-security response could cut global oil demand by 4% by 2035. Without Iranian oil, China's small refiners face pain but not collapse. (Headlines: Reuters 11-19, 11-20, 11-21; AP 11-21; Bloomberg 11-19, 11-20; WSJ 11-21; FT 11-21; Al Jazeera 11-17, 11-20, 11-21; CNBC 11-21; TV5Monde 11-17; BBC 11-21.)

DIPLOMACY AND TALKS: Despite the fighting, diplomacy continued in parallel. A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on November 21 for talks. Iran's foreign minister Araqchi said Iran wants diplomacy to end the war, but Trump said the terms are unacceptable. Trump said there is no rush on an Iran decision and he looks to next year. He said he wants a permanent deal to stop Iran getting nuclear weapons. Pakistan vowed to proceed with US-Iran diplomacy. Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchanged fire. The West pressed Iran at the IAEA to let inspections resume at bombed nuclear sites. The US, China, and Russia clashed over the nuclear stalemate. (Headlines: Reuters 11-20, 11-21; AP 11-20; Bloomberg 11-19; Al Jazeera 11-21; FT 11-20; WSJ 11-16; TV5Monde 11-15; Reuters 11-19.)

IRAQ AND PRO-IRAN MILITIAS: Iraq's government moved to crack down on Iran-backed militias. Iraqi security forces deployed to Jurf al-Sakhar, the stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah, after reaching a compromise with the group. The Iraqi leader's planned crackdown was described as his riskiest move yet. A top IRGC commander visited Iraq for talks. An Iran-backed group warned Iraqi forces against entering its stronghold. The militia rakes in hundreds of millions through oil smuggling. (Headlines: Reuters 11-19, 11-20; AP 11-17, 11-20; Al Jazeera 11-16, 11-20; TV5Monde 11-17; Reuters 11-16.)

SANCTIONS AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE: The US Treasury sanctioned Iranian trustees collecting oil revenues and a Hezbollah-linked charity. The US pressed Singapore and Malaysia on sanctions compliance. The US tightened its blockade with curbs on oil transfers at sea. Iranian oil leverage is weakening, which could push Tehran toward escalation. The US-Iran deal uncertainty weighed on the rupee and bonds. (Headlines: Reuters 11-18, 11-20; Al Jazeera 11-18, 11-19, 11-20; Bloomberg 11-19; Reuters 11-16.)

DOMESTIC IRAN: Iranian leaders fretted over public mood as gas shortages added to the war's ills. Iran will ration electricity despite its vast gas and oil reserves. A protest broke out in a southwestern town after a road crash killed 13 refinery workers. Iranian women are reclaiming their freedom to dress as they please. More educated young Iranians no longer see their future at home. Bloomberg ran a piece titled The Iranian Revolution Hiding in Plain Sight, suggesting internal transformation. A graphic memoir documented a woman's life under protests and war. (Headlines: Reuters 11-16, 11-19; TV5Monde 11-21; DW 11-21, 11-16; Bloomberg 11-20; AP 11-19.)

US DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE WAR: Congress struggled to avert a US shutdown as the Iran war divided lawmakers. Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic resolution to limit Trump's war powers. Trump defended the war in his Veterans Day address and said it played a role in the midterms. VP Vance declined to say he would have ordered Iran strikes, and Trump initially appeared angry before defending their friendship. The war cost surpassed 48 billion dollars, with lawmakers demanding unreleased estimates on base damage. (Headlines: Reuters 11-20; AP 11-19, 11-20; CNN 11-20; Bloomberg 11-20; WSJ 11-20; FT 11-20; DW 11-20; Al Jazeera 11-19.)

ASSASSINATION PLOTS AND ESPIONAGE: North Macedonia and Greece uncovered an Iran-linked assassination plot. A Pakistani man was sentenced to over 27 years in a US prison for an assassination plot targeting Trump that he said was steered from Iran. An Iranian operative accused of directing a failed terror plot at a US base declared innocence. Two men will stand trial in the UK next year over an RAF Fairford incident allegedly linked to Iran. (Headlines: Reuters 11-17, 11-18; AP 11-17, 11-18; BBC 11-18; CNN 11-18, 11-19; Al Jazeera 11-19.)

ISRAEL'S ROLE: Israel's spy chief lobbied for joint Iran strikes during a US visit. Israel urged renewed Iran strikes. Israel pivoted to cheaper air defense as Iran tensions rose. Mideast nations ramped up efforts to avert all-out war while Israel pushed for strikes. (Headlines: Reuters 11-18; AP 11-19; Bloomberg 11-20; WSJ 11-19; Al Jazeera 11-19.)

BAHRAIN AND GULF ALLIES: Bahrain intercepted multiple Iranian aerial attacks, with the IRGC claiming it targeted a US radar. Scores of Bahraini Shia clerics were given life sentences, accused of plotting with Iran. Kuwait repelled Iranian attacks. Gulf countries were under fire after the US hit Qeshm. The UAE is conducting risky Hormuz operations. (Headlines: Reuters 11-15, 11-16, 11-17, 11-21; BBC 11-15, 11-18; FT 11-16, 11-18; Al Jazeera 11-17, 11-18; TV5Monde 11-15, 11-17, 11-18; WSJ 11-21.)
