crystal.eli5:
Switzerland is having a big argument about whether it should sell more weapons to other countries. This is a really old question for them because Switzerland has always said it stays out of other countries' fights. Last week, young people marched in the streets saying they want to keep that promise, and the whole country is watching the final vote. In the next few days, you will see the result and everyone reacting, and then the story will mostly go away, which is how Swiss votes work: big bang, then quiet.

At the same time, the big bank UBS is in a fight with the government about how much money the bank has to keep in reserve as a safety cushion. Last week, the bank basically said, okay, you win, but let us change a few details. So next week the story becomes more boring and more legal: lawyers, committee meetings, and the little family offices that manage rich people's money trying to convince parliament that they can police themselves. It is less like a boxing match and more like a long, slow negotiation.

The thing that surprised people last week is that young Swiss people are getting more loud and more political. They marched against spending more on the military, and a big group of men marched for women's rights. This is not like the old Switzerland where everyone agreed quietly behind closed doors. Next week, if the weapons vote goes a direction the young people do not like, expect more marching, more social media, and more politicians trying to sound young. The football team also just crushed Scotland four-nil, so the mood is a bit more cheerful than it was last week, and the league matches will keep the sports pages busy.

One small thing to watch: a Swiss group that investigates how the world works published a report saying the United Arab Emirates is a big stop for gold that was not supposed to leave Africa legally. The UAE might get a little annoyed, and the Swiss trade minister might have to say something. It is not a huge story, but it shows Switzerland still likes to keep score on the world's messy trade, even while it argues with itself about what kind of country it wants to be.

measurement.happened: The dominant story of the week in Singapore was the Nvidia chip scandal and its fallout. Multiple outlets reported that Nvidia had been using Singapore as a key routing point for AI chips destined for China, and that the company had stopped disclosing its Singapore sales figures even as its total revenues hit 104 billion dollars. The Financial Times ran a detailed piece on how Jensen Huang's family had shaped Nvidia's Singapore dealings, suggesting personal and business ties went deeper than a simple distribution hub. Singapore's Prime Minister Wong publicly acknowledged that the new US chip curbs would have 'some impact' on the city-state. Singapore then moved to seek what it called 'trusted access' to AI chips under the new US restrictions, and Reuters reported that Singapore and the US agreed to keep discussing a framework called Megaspeed while scrutiny of the Nvidia scandal widened. Bloomberg noted that crowded Singapore bank stocks faced rotation as AI risks mounted, signalling that the financial sector was feeling the tremors. In short, Singapore found itself at the center of a US-China chip tug-of-war, and the government was in active damage control mode, trying to preserve its position as a trusted intermediary without looking like it was helping China dodge restrictions. The second major theme was the Indonesian wildfire haze. Indonesia's President Prabowo formally apologized to Singapore and Malaysia for the smog that had been drifting across the region. The apology was reported by Reuters, Bloomberg, and Al Jazeera on November 15 and 16. However, Deutsche Welle reported on November 20 that the forest fires were still spewing smoky haze over Singapore and Malaysia, meaning the problem was not yet fully resolved despite the diplomatic gesture. Singaporeans continued to deal with degraded air quality, and the episode reinforced the perennial tension between Singapore and its larger neighbor over transboundary pollution. The third theme was Singapore's broader financial and business activity. Bloomberg reported that Singapore-based DayOne paused its US IPO plans citing data center and market concerns, a sign that the tech-fintech funding window may be narrowing. On a positive note, Singapore's property market saw sales hit a year-high, and the sovereign wealth fund teamed with Saudi Telecom to bid for a UK data center stake. Quantitative trading firm Graviton expanded its offices in both Singapore and India, and a Singapore profit surge minted two new Indian billionaires. India's Paytm partnered with Singapore's Funding Societies in a deal worth up to 21 million dollars, and NETS deepened its partnership with Ant International around agentic commerce and mobile payments. Singapore also urged deeper ASEAN ties in AI and energy as it prepares to take the ASEAN chair in 2027, signaling its ambition to lead regional digital and energy policy. In the cybersecurity space, SentinelOne and Singapore's Digital and Intelligence Service announced a partnership to strengthen cyber defense and advance secure AI, a notable signal that the government is investing in next-generation digital security. The US Treasury separately pressed Singapore and Malaysia on Iran sanctions compliance, suggesting that Singapore's role as a global financial hub is under closer regulatory watch, particularly regarding how transactions linked to Iran flow through its banks. On the sports front, Singapore hosted a football event that ended in humiliation: Brazil crushed the local side 7-0, with Vinicius Jr scoring a first-half hat-trick. The match was covered by Reuters, AP, and Al Jazeera. Earlier in the week, Japan had stunned Brazil 3-2 in Singapore in another match, suggesting this was some kind of friendly tournament or exhibition series. The WTA Singapore Open tennis tournament was also underway, with the BBC tracking scores and schedules. In aviation, a Singapore Airlines jet had to U-turn after a second cabin smoke incident, raising fresh questions about safety protocols. A smaller cultural note: AFP profiled the opening of Moutai House in Singapore, a Chinese baijiu brand's cultural and retail presence in the city. An Indian driver also won a 1.3 million dollar lottery prize in Singapore, a feel-good story that made the BBC. Overall, the week was defined by Singapore's central but uncomfortable role in the US-China tech rivalry, the ongoing haze nuisance from Indonesia, and a busy undercurrent of financial deals, sports, and institutional partnerships.

crystal.eli5:
Think of Singapore like a tiny, super-smart middleman sitting between two very big, very powerful friends who are arguing. One friend (the US) wants to make sure the other friend (China) does not get too many fancy computer chips. Singapore has been helping the chips get from one friend to the other, and now everyone is asking: 'Are you sure you are not helping the other friend cheat?' So next week, Singapore is going to sit down with the US and try to write a rulebook that says, 'Here is how we can keep trading chips in a fair, trusted way.' It is like two kids arguing over a toy, and the small kid in the middle has to explain why they are allowed to hold the toy.

At the same time, the air is still smoky because of fires in Indonesia. The Indonesian president already said sorry, which is nice, but the smoke has not gone away. So Singaporeans will still be coughing and wearing masks, and the governments will probably have another meeting to figure out how to actually stop the fires, not just apologize for them. It is like your neighbor saying 'Sorry about the smoke' but still not turning off the barbecue.

In the business world, a lot of deals keep happening every week. New companies sign partnerships, new data centers get planned, new payment systems get built. It is like a very busy marketplace where the specific stalls change every week but the market itself is always full of people. One company that wanted to go public in the US paused its plans, which is a small signal that the funding mood might be cooling. And the property market is doing well, with sales at a yearly high, so people are still buying homes.

Singapore Airlines also had a second weird problem where smoke appeared in a plane's cabin, and the plane had to turn around and land. Two times in a row is a lot, so the airline will probably have to explain what is going on and make sure passengers feel safe. It is like your favorite restaurant having a food-safety issue twice in a week; you want to know they fixed it before you go back.

And there is a tennis tournament happening, and a football match where Singapore lost by a lot. These are smaller stories, but they keep the sports pages busy and give people something to talk about at lunch.

measurement.happened:
This week in Brazil was dominated by a cluster of major stories that together paint a picture of a country in political transition, economic stress, and cultural reckoning.

Bolsonaro's Health Crisis. The single most dominant story of the week was the hospitalization of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Starting on November 20, Bolsonaro was admitted with intestinal obstruction and abdominal pain, and by November 21 he had been moved to the ICU. Reuters, Bloomberg, CNN, Deutsche Welle, Al Jazeera, and TV5Monde all covered the admission. His son confirmed the hospitalization publicly. This is not the first time Bolsonaro has been hospitalized, but the ICU admission raises immediate questions about his capacity to lead the opposition and whether he will survive another round of political combat. The timing is awkward: he is in the hospital while Lula is consolidating a fourth term, which weakens the main face of the right-wing opposition at a critical moment.

Lula's Fourth Term and the Fiscal Package. Multiple sources confirm that Lula has won re-election for a fourth term. AP notes that 'Lula will govern Brazil for a fourth term but faces a range of challenges.' Deutsche Welle reports that Germany's Merz and other world leaders congratulated Lula. AFP simply filed a headline reading 'Brazil elections 2026,' confirming the event. The immediate policy priority has been fiscal: the Senate approved a roughly $10 billion fiscal package on November 18, as reported by Reuters and AP. The finance minister signaled on November 18 that additional fiscal measures would come 'in the near term' and admitted on November 17 that the tax reform would have an initial inflationary impact. Bloomberg's headline on November 19 is blunt: 'Lula Is Heading Straight for Brazil's Fiscal Cliff.' The WSJ also noted on November 16 that Lula is entering Spain's election fray, suggesting he is trying to project regional leadership while his own fiscal position is under strain.

Economic and Market Turmoil. The fiscal worries have hit Brazilian markets hard. Bloomberg reported on November 19 that the central bank stepped into markets as fiscal woes hit the real, and on November 16 that the real led FX losses among emerging-market currencies. Banks are literally swapping Brazil for Mexico in regional equity picks (Bloomberg, Nov 19). Bradesco's CEO called for 'prudence' at Brazilian banks. A billionaire named Bishop put $300 million into an ailing Brazilian bank (Nov 17). The B3 exchange is adding Brazil stocks listed abroad to try to prop up the local market. Analysts lifted both key-rate and inflation forecasts on fiscal risk (Nov 16). BlackRock bought SulAmérica to expand its Latin America reach, a sign that foreign investors are still looking for value but are being selective. The overall picture is one of a currency under pressure, a banking sector on edge, and a government scrambling to show fiscal discipline.

Indigenous and Amazon Stories. Two related threads ran through the week. First, rare images and video of the Awá, an isolated Indigenous group in the Amazon, surfaced. The Awá broke their isolation to ask for food, which raised urgent concerns about their safety and the threats they face (Reuters Nov 17, AP Nov 18, TV5Monde Nov 19, Al Jazeera Nov 18). Second, Lula personally visited the ailing Indigenous leader Chief Raoni in hospital, and Brazil formally recognized the territory around Raoni's birthplace. Raoni had been in hospital for five days before leaving (TV5Monde Nov 18). Reuters, AP, AFP, and Al Jazeera all covered the visit and the territorial recognition. This is both a symbolic gesture and a policy move, reinforcing Lula's environmental and Indigenous-rights brand heading into his fourth term. Canada and the UK (via Carney) pledged up to $392.5 million / C$560 million for a Brazil-led tropical forest fund (Reuters Nov 15, Bloomberg Nov 15), tying the Amazon story to international climate finance.

Football Drama. Brazil's national team had a turbulent week in Singapore. They lost 3-2 to Japan in a shocker, with Carlo Ancelotti and Raphinha both sent off in stoppage time (Reuters Nov 14, AP Nov 14, Al Jazeera Nov 15). Legend Romario called for Ancelotti to be sacked (BBC Nov 17). Then, in a follow-up friendly, Brazil crushed Singapore 7-0 with Vinicius Jr scoring a first-half hat-trick (Reuters Nov 17, AP Nov 17, Al Jazeera Nov 17). Ronaldinho, at 46, returned to club football with third-division Ravenna (AP Nov 15). A brawl erupted in the Women's League final (Al Jazeera Nov 15). The U17 team is preparing for a World Cup match against Ireland (BBC Nov 20). The football story is a mix of embarrassment, redemption, and nostalgia.

Storm Damage. A severe storm hit a Brazilian town, destroying thousands of homes and killing three people. AFP reported on November 21 that residents were clearing rubble and saying 'we lost everything.' This adds a human-cost weather story to an already busy week.

Trade, Investment, and Business. China's Jetour (under Chery) reached a deal to produce vehicles in Brazil starting in 2027 with a $69 million investment (Reuters Nov 17-18). Brazil formally contested the EU's review of Anglo American's nickel mine sale to China's MMG (Reuters Nov 17). Prio and ExxonMobil won lots in a PPSA spot oil auction (Reuters Nov 16). Aclara is weighing a rare-earth plant in Brazil (Bloomberg Nov 18). Labcorp is expanding clinical trial operations in Brazil through a partnership with Grupo Fleury (FT Nov 17). Ant International's Alipay+ will connect over 50 global e-wallets with Pix (AFP Nov 19). The corn ethanol boom is accelerating feedlot beef growth (Reuters Nov 19). Nestle's Brazilian coffee supplier faced a hearing over labor abuse claims (Reuters Nov 16). Ten employees were injured in a boiler explosion at a Klabin paper factory (Reuters Nov 18). Brazil's prosecutors sued Shell for $108 million over the deadly 2024 floods (AFP Nov 18). The WSJ ran a piece on the bitter feud between the leaders of Brazil and Argentina going global (Nov 17).

Political Color. TV5Monde reported on November 21 that André Janones, described as Lula's re-election strategist, is exploring the limits of the 'ethically doubtful,' suggesting some internal friction or controversy around the election campaign's methods. This adds a layer of political drama beneath the surface.

The fiscal narrative also grew sharply: what was a package being unveiled and debated became a Senate-approved $10 billion measure on November 18, but the framing shifted from 'Lula showing discipline' to Bloomberg's blunt 'Lula Is Heading Straight for Brazil's Fiscal Cliff,' and the finance minister himself admitted the tax reform would be initially inflationary. Market stress deepened in kind and degree: the first photograph showed anxiety and a currency near its low; the second shows the central bank actively stepping into FX markets, banks literally swapping Brazil for Mexico in regional equity picks, a billionaire injecting $300 million into an ailing bank, and the B3 exchange adding foreign-listed Brazilian stocks to prop up the local market. The Amazon and Indigenous thread expanded from a single Norway $64 million gift into a cluster: Canada and the UK pledging up to $392.5 million for a Brazil-led tropical forest fund, the Awá people breaking their isolation to ask for food, and Lula personally visiting Chief Raoni in hospital before Brazil formally recognizing the territory around Raoni's birthplace. Football moved from a single embarrassing 3-2 loss to a full emotional arc: Romario publicly calling for Ancelotti's sacking, then a 7-0 demolition of Singapore with a Vinicius hat-trick, plus a brawl in the Women's League final and U17 World Cup preparations. A new weather story appeared from nothing: a severe storm that destroyed thousands of homes and killed three people. Trade and investment broadened from scattered corporate stories into a visible cluster of new entrants: China's Jetour committing $69 million to produce vehicles in Brazil from 2027, Alipay+ connecting over 50 global e-wallets to Pix, Aclara weighing a rare-earth plant, and Prio and ExxonMobil winning PPSA auction lots. What shrank or vanished: the BP-Petrobras stake-sale talks, the Meta fine follow-up, the Braskem debt-deadline drama, the WEG Mexico investment, the Nubank and Agibank individual stories, the Paraguay dam bank scandal, the smuggled-pesticide investigation, the Franklin Templeton risk-trim, and the Norwegian Amazon Fund (superseded by the larger Canada-UK pledge) all disappeared from the second photograph as if they had never been. The first photograph was a week of scattered, multi-threaded news; the second is a week where a handful of dominant stories (Bolsonaro's health, the fiscal cliff, the Awá/Raoni Amazon cluster, the football embarrassment-and-redemption arc) absorbed or swallowed the smaller threads that had filled the first week's space.

delta.driver: The force pushing Brazil from the first photograph to the second is the collision of a political transition with an economy that does not have the fiscal space to absorb the transition's promises. Lula's fourth term is now a fact, not a prospect, and the Senate has approved the initial fiscal package, but the market is reading the gap between the package and the fiscal cliff as a credibility problem, and that credibility problem is showing up in the currency, in the banking sector, and in foreign investor allocation decisions almost in real time. Bolsonaro's ICU admission is not a random medical event; it is the physical manifestation of a right-wing opposition that is politically exhausted, personally fractured, and now led by a man who may not survive the next round of combat in the body. The Amazon cluster (Awá, Raoni, Canada-UK fund) is driven by Lula's need to anchor his fourth term in a recognizable brand and by international climate finance that is looking for a post-2015 framework, and it is also driven by the simple fact that isolated peoples are breaking contact and that a beloved elder is dying, which makes the political symbolism impossible to ignore. The football arc is driven by the same national psychology that drives the fiscal narrative: a deep fear of losing, a quick pivot to redemption, and a nostalgia for a simpler past (Ronaldinho at 46) that the present cannot quite deliver. The storm is the reminder that the physical infrastructure of the country is still vulnerable, and that the fiscal and political stories are being lived by people clearing rubble. Underneath all of this is a single thread: a country trying to govern a fourth term while its currency, its banks, its opposition, and its forests are all in a state of active stress, and the speed at which each of those stress points escalates or resolves is what will determine whether the next photograph looks like consolidation or crisis.

crystal.headline: Bolsonaro in ICU as Brazil's Fiscal Cliff Deepens
emoji_reasons: Bolsonaro's ICU admission is the week's dominant political story and the opposition's fate hangs on his condition.
The fiscal cliff, currency pressure, and banking anxiety will continue to drive economic headlines and market moves.
Football's emotional arc from humiliation to redemption will produce another round of drama, sacking calls, or a viral moment.
crystal.tldr: Bolsonaro's ICU stay will dominate political news while his condition determines whether the opposition rallies or fractures. The fiscal and market story continues with the real under pressure, the central bank defending it, and the finance minister promising more measures. Football, the Awá, the storm's rubble, and a scattering of trade announcements fill the rest of the week.
crystal.eli5:
Brazil's former president, Jair Bolsonaro, is in the intensive care unit of a hospital with a serious stomach and intestine problem. This is the biggest story of the week because he is the face of the political opposition, and nobody knows if he will get better or worse. His son has to talk to the cameras, and the people who disagree with the current government are either rallying around him or worrying that he might not be able to lead them for a while.

The economy is also under a lot of stress. The government just passed a plan to save about ten billion dollars in the budget, but experts and investors think that is not enough. The Brazilian money, called the real, is getting weaker, and the central bank has to step in to stop it from falling too fast. Some banks are getting nervous, and one rich person had to put three hundred million dollars into a struggling bank to keep it from looking too shaky. The government says more money-saving measures are coming, but the markets are not fully convinced yet.

In the Amazon, a very rare group of Indigenous people called the Awá came out of the forest for the first time in a long time to ask for food. That is both a beautiful and a worrying story, because it means they are in trouble. The current president also visited a very old and beloved Indigenous chief who is sick in the hospital, and the government officially protected the land where the chief was born. Canada and the United Kingdom promised nearly four hundred million dollars to help protect Brazil's forests, which is a big deal for climate.

On the football side, Brazil lost a shocking game to Japan, then won a big one against Singapore, and a famous retired player who is now forty-six years old went back to playing for a small club. The country is still arguing about whether the coach should stay or go. And a bad storm destroyed thousands of houses in one town and killed three people, so families are still picking through the rubble trying to find what they lost.

The real's slide, the central bank's market intervention, the Senate's fiscal package, and banks swapping Brazil for Mexico all point to a week of clear economic and market stress.
Lula's visit to Raoni, the formal recognition of Indigenous territory, and the rare Awá encounter make the Amazon and Brazil's Indigenous peoples the moral and environmental center of the week.

measurement.happened:
The single dominant story in Australia this week was the eruption of what the media has dubbed 'Sandpapergate,' a resurgent and deeply uncomfortable ball-tampering scandal in Australian cricket. Cameron Bancroft, one of the central figures in the 2018 plot, publicly claimed that the 'entire Australian team' was aware of the sandpaper plot, a statement that sent shockwaves through the sport (Reuters, AP, AFP, Al Jazeera, BBC). Cricket Australia responded by setting up a player forum and a 'safe space' for players to share their experiences, while explicitly ruling out a formal probe (Al Jazeera, BBC). The federal government, under pressure, urged Cricket Australia to ensure transparency in the forum process (Reuters, Al Jazeera). Former coach Darren Lehmann again denied knowing about the plot while he was in charge, and ex-bowler Sayers said everyone on the squad was in on it (BBC, AFP). David Warner accused Cricket Australia of a 'cover-up,' and both Warner and Usman Khawaja were taken off broadcast duties for the England series (Al Jazeera). Despite the chaos, Cricket Australia gave Pat Cummins 'unanimous support' to remain Test captain, with Hazlewood and others publicly backing him (Reuters, AFP, BBC, Al Jazeera). On the field, the fallout was visible: England thrashed Australia in the ODI series, with Duckett hitting a century in the decisive match, but Australia bounced back to win the T20 series opener thanks to Nikhil Chaudhary (Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, Al Jazeera). The Sandpapergate story consumed an extraordinary share of headlines across all twelve sources, appearing in roughly thirty of the one hundred thirteen items, making it by far the week's defining narrative.

The second major theme was economic strain. Australia's unemployment rate jumped to 4.9 percent, the highest in five years, following the Reserve Bank's recent rate-hike cycle, and markets immediately ramped up bets on rate cuts in 2027 (Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ). Australian stocks posted their worst week since 2022, with miners leading the tumble (Bloomberg). The Australian dollar was set to give back its 2026 gain on those rate-cut expectations (Bloomberg). Corporate Australia saw further job cuts, with KPMG Australia trimming an additional 230 roles amid its ongoing scandal, and a broader pattern of corporate headcount reductions across the country (Reuters). The iconic department store David Jones, with debts now topping 300 million dollars, was actively seeking buyers, a story picked up by both Reuters and Bloomberg as a symbol of retail stress (Reuters, Bloomberg). On a slightly brighter note, the gender pay gap declined to its lowest level on record (Bloomberg), and wage growth quickened, which complicates the inflation picture the RBA is managing (Bloomberg). Housing auction clearances slumped to a six-year low as rates stayed elevated (Bloomberg). The overall picture was of an economy that had overheated, is now cooling unevenly, and is leaving some workers and businesses behind.

China-Australia relations occupied a third major thread. Prime Minister Albanese met President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit, and both leaders hailed a 'comprehensive turnaround' in bilateral ties (Reuters, AP, DW, FT, Bloomberg). However, the warmth was undercut by ongoing trade friction: Australia launched an investigation into alleged Chinese timber dumping, hardened its stance on China's efforts to influence iron-ore pricing, and warned that Beijing's iron-ore push could breach trade rules (Bloomberg, WSJ). The WSJ framed it as China 'flexing muscle' in iron ore, squeezing Australian miners. On the security side, Australia and the Philippines signed an upgraded defence pact explicitly aimed at countering China's regional influence (Reuters, Bloomberg), and CNBC noted that President Trump was set to meet with the Quad countries including Australia (CNBC). The net effect was a relationship that is diplomatically warmer but commercially and strategically more tense than the headlines suggest.

Artificial intelligence and technology formed a fourth cluster. Anthropic's planned Australian data centre drew overwhelming opposition from local residents (Reuters), and the company's IPO raised only 110 million dollars from Australian investors, a modest figure that Bloomberg's AustralianSuper CIO compared to dot-com-bubble dynamics (Bloomberg). The Commonwealth Bank announced it was investing in its own compute power for an AI push, citing Australia's growing attractiveness on compute availability (Bloomberg). TechnologyOne, a major Australian software firm, said it was resisting the wave of AI-driven job cuts to boost productivity instead (Reuters). The government vowed to regulate AI agent shoppers and surveillance pricing, a new consumer-protection frontier (Bloomberg). Pension funds were confronting the challenge of AI agents in investment advice, and the government moved to allow those funds to offer more targeted advice and unlock new investment through a revamped regulatory test (Bloomberg). Energy officials reportedly warned of risks from data-centre electricity demand (Bloomberg). The theme was one of excitement and anxiety in equal measure.

In other sports, Australia delivered a dominant performance in rugby league, crushing New Zealand 32-12 to win a fourth consecutive Rugby League World Cup, while the women's team, Clinical Australia, beat New Zealand to claim a thirteenth World Cup title (Reuters, AP, AFP, Al Jazeera). In rugby union, the Wallabies lost to Scotland 15-12 in the Nations Championship, their fourth straight defeat, a result that drew criticism of the team's arm-wrestling style (AP, AFP, BBC, TV5Monde). A pair of Melbourne Cup stories added a touch of local colour and outrage: the horse So You Are was found dead in a waste facility, triggering an inquiry, and Victoria Police arrested a man over the theft of Makybe Diva's three Melbourne Cup trophies (AP). The wreck of Australia's first domestically built warship was found 128 years after it sank, a small but poignant maritime-history moment (AP).

On the political and security front, the US sanctioned the Australian branch of the Comanchero motorcycle gang over drug-trafficking links (Reuters). A Sydney man was charged with a car-bomb plot and downloading Islamic State material (AP). Injured federal lawmaker Helen Haines left hospital after an alleged SUV attack, a reminder of the physical risks facing politicians (AP). Australia sanctioned Israeli settlers and organisations over West Bank expansion, and joined Canada, Italy, and the UK in urging Israel to allow aid into Gaza (Reuters, Al Jazeera). The High Court delivered a landmark ruling against a coal mine in a climate case, a decision that DW framed as part of Australia's broader 'climate dilemma of selling nature while exporting coal' (AFP, DW). The government also moved to require backpacker visa holders to do extra rural work to ease the labour crunch (Reuters, Bloomberg).

In corporate and financial news, Mayne Pharma jumped to a one-year high after Gedeon Richter agreed to a 408-million-dollar takeover (Reuters). IDP Education rebuffed Blackstone's third buyout attempt at a 564.5-million-dollar valuation (Reuters). An RRJ-led consortium bought a coal miner's 619-million-dollar debt, a sign of financial stress in the sector (Bloomberg). The US fracking hopeful hired American heavyweights for a sensitive Western Australia project (Reuters). Australia freed its largest LNG-exporting state from the reservation scheme, though negotiations on the gas reservation proposal were still ongoing (Reuters, Bloomberg). Chevron's Australia president commented on Hormuz disruptions and LNG demand (CNBC).

measurement.happened:
The dominant story of the week in Indonesia was the signing of a comprehensive trade deal with the European Union after a full decade of negotiations. The EU member-state governments authorised the signature on November 18 (Reuters, Al Jazeera), and the actual signing took place on November 21 (Reuters, Deutsche Welle). The agreement covers everything from palm oil to pharmaceuticals (Deutsche Welle) and is widely framed as a strategic response to the tariff environment created by the United States (Al Jazeera). For a country that has long courted both blocs, locking in a free-trade framework with the EU while simultaneously deepening ties with China gives Prabowo Subianto a broader diplomatic hand to play. The deal is likely to be the single most consequential economic event for Indonesia in years, and it will dominate headlines for weeks as implementation details emerge.

The second major thread was the rupiah crisis. The currency hit record lows against the dollar on November 16 (Bloomberg), and the Bank Indonesia resumed rate hikes on November 18, a move that surprised many analysts (Bloomberg, WSJ, Reuters). The rate decision was described as a close call (Bloomberg), and analysts warned the central bank faces an uphill battle to stem the slide (Bloomberg). The political turmoil, including the wiretapping scandal, was explicitly cited as adding to market anxiety and a potential MSCI reclassification risk (Reuters). The rupiah weakness is not just a macro issue; it raises import costs for fuel, food, and raw materials, which feeds directly into inflation and the cost of living for hundreds of millions of Indonesians.

The wiretapping scandal consumed the political centre of gravity. On November 17, police dismissed at least two senior officials, including a general, over suspicions that the president's communications had been tapped (Reuters, AP). The AFP reported that a protest video was misrepresented online as a build-up of forces at the national police headquarters, showing how quickly the story mutated in the social-media sphere. Deutsche Welle reported that troops were deployed to Jakarta in the wake of the allegations, a significant and somewhat unusual move that signalled the government took the threat seriously. The ex-president's court appearance was falsely linked to the scandal by some outlets (AFP), adding to the noise. The overall picture is one of a president whose own security apparatus may have been listening to him, with the credibility of the police force and the ruling coalition now in question.

On the environmental and regional front, the annual forest-fire haze returned. Prabowo personally apologised to Singapore and Malaysia on November 15 (Reuters, DW, FT, Al Jazeera), but by November 17 he was also shifting blame, telling the press it was not entirely Indonesia's fault (CNN). Deutsche Welle reported on November 20 that the fires were still spewing smog over both neighbours, and a new sanctuary for rescued orangutans was announced (AFP). Indonesian farmers took an unusual and vivid form of protest, cementing their own feet to the ground (DW), underscoring how the fires and the economic squeeze are hitting the rural population hard.

Indonesia's relationship with China moved into a new gear. Prabowo and Xi discussed future cooperation in the South China Sea (Reuters), and the two countries announced four strategic partnerships worth 71.8 billion dollars (Reuters). At the same time, Indonesia is planning tighter control over soybean imports, which are largely US-sourced (Reuters, Bloomberg), a move that will be read in Washington as a subtle signal. The resource-nationalism thread continued: the government said 70 percent of benefits from mines should go to the state (Bloomberg), it revoked a forest permit from billionaire Surya Paloh's associate Tanoto's firm (Bloomberg), and Franky Widjaja resigned as commissioner of a major palm-oil company (Bloomberg). PT Freeport Indonesia priced a 750-million-dollar senior notes offering (FT), showing the mining sector is still raising capital despite the political risk premium.

In the tech and media space, Google removed 19,000 YouTube channels that were identified as pro-government (Bloomberg), and the Indonesian communications ministry asked Google to clarify the removals (Reuters). Separately, the Straits Times reported that Indonesian police had raided the local unit of Nvidia partner Megaspeed in early 2026 at the US request (Reuters), a detail that adds a layer of great-power tech rivalry to an already tense relationship with Washington. Three people were also arrested in a probe into the manipulation of warrant transactions (Reuters), a smaller but notable financial-crime story.

Smaller but newsworthy items included a magnitude 5.9 earthquake on Flores (Reuters), an explosion at an oil refinery that killed one worker (Reuters), a train colliding with a minibus (Al Jazeera), the resumption of macaque exports for animal testing (DW), a daycare principal jailed for five years over child abuse (BBC), and the passage of the long-debated asset-forfeiture law by parliament (Reuters, Bloomberg), which gives the state a new tool to seize assets linked to corruption and other crimes without a full criminal conviction.

I expect the Ministry of Finance and the Attorney General's office to issue technical guidelines, and the business community, particularly conglomerates with complex asset structures, to lobby for transitional provisions. I rate a high-profile first seizure or a test case as unlikely within one week but possible if a pending case is fast-tracked.

The Google/YouTube channel removal will likely prompt a formal written response from Google to the Indonesian ministry, and the communications ministry may hold a press briefing. I rate a regulatory hearing or a draft amendment to the digital-services rules as possible but not certain within this week. The Megaspeed/Nvidia raid story will see further reporting as the Straits Times and local outlets dig into the scope of the US request, but I do not expect a formal diplomatic protest within the week.

Less likely surprises I would keep on the radar: a second major natural disaster (another earthquake or a volcanic eruption) that briefly steals the headline; a sudden foreign-exchange intervention by the central bank that moves the rupiah by more than two percent in a single session; a parliamentary vote or motion of no-confidence triggered by the wiretapping fallout; or a new round of forest-fire smoke that forces schools in Jakarta to close. Each of these is possible but I would not assign them more than a one-in-four chance.

These are all within the realm of possibility over a longer horizon, but for a single week I would put them in the unlikely-to-improbable range.

delta.motion: The most striking shift between the two photographs is the replacement of the vice-presidential resignation as the dominant narrative. In the first week, Gibran's departure, the 120-lawmaker impeachment motion, and the December 2 upper-house vote consumed the political frame. By the second week, the VP vacancy has receded into the background; the formal vote is still ahead, but the story has been overtaken by the signing of the EU trade deal, a decade-long negotiation that lands as the single biggest economic headline. The wiretapping scandal, by contrast, accelerated sharply. It moved from 'police say they have enough evidence for treason charges' to two senior officials including a general being dismissed, troops being deployed to Jakarta, and a protest video being misrepresented online as a military build-up at police headquarters. The escalation from legal procedure to personnel purge and security mobilization happened faster than the first photograph suggested. The rupiah crisis deepened: the currency that hit a record low in week one hit a new record low in week two, and the Bank of Indonesia responded with a surprise rate hike on November 18, a move that was not part of the first week's picture at all. The wildfire theme shifted from a domestic climate-and-enforcement story to an international diplomatic one: Prabowo personally apologized to Singapore and Malaysia, then within two days was telling the press the fires were not entirely Indonesia's fault, while smog was still spilling over both neighbors and farmers in the affected regions took to cementing their own feet to the ground in protest. The China relationship grew from a collection of smaller trade items (coal contract disputes, an LNG plant investment) into a full strategic realignment: Prabowo and Xi discussed South China Sea cooperation, and four partnerships worth 71.8 billion dollars were announced. Resource nationalism, which in week one was a presidential order to give the state a bigger share of mining benefits, hardened in week two into a 70-percent state-benefit rule, the revocation of a forest permit linked to billionaire Tanoto, and the resignation of a commissioner at a major palm-oil company. The tech-and-media theme changed shape: week one was about Meta, TikTok, and Google pushing back on AI copyright revisions; week two is about Google removing 19,000 pro-government YouTube channels and police raiding the local unit of Nvidia partner Megaspeed at the US request, a shift from domestic copyright policy to great-power tech rivalry. What vanished or shrank noticeably: the MSCI index changes that were a headline in week one are reduced to a background reclassification risk in week two; the panda bond, the BP petrol-station stake sale, the Norway carbon-offset deal, the Eramet nickel-mine bid, and the September retail-sales figure all disappear from the second photograph. The earthquake that displaced 13,000 people in week one is replaced by a smaller 5.9 on Flores in week two. New items that had no counterpart in the first photograph include the EU trade deal itself, the Bank of Indonesia rate hike, the troop deployment to Jakarta, the asset-forfeiture law passing parliament, the oil-refinery explosion, the train-minibus collision, the resumption of macaque exports for animal testing, and the daycare principal's five-year jail sentence. delta.driver: The force moving Indonesia from the first photograph to the second is a government under internal political stress using the window of crisis to accelerate two simultaneous projects: consolidating power at home and diversifying its economic partnerships abroad. The wiretapping scandal and the VP ouster have created a credibility gap around the presidency and the police, and the government's response has been to tighten the security perimeter (dismissals, troop deployment) while the political elite jostle for the VP slot and the wiretapping fallout. At the same time, the weak rupiah and the US tariff environment are pushing Jakarta to lock in new trade frameworks before the dollar keeps sliding, which is why the decade-long EU negotiation was brought to a signature in this exact moment and why the China partnerships and South China Sea talks were elevated to a strategic level. Resource nationalism is the connective tissue: the 70-percent state-benefit rule, the Tanoto permit revocation, and the mining-benefits order are all expressions of a government that wants to extract more value from its own ground before foreign partners and domestic elites capture it. The wildfires are the constant physical pressure that keeps public anger high and makes every policy failure more visible, while the EU deal and the China deals are the government's answer to the question 'what do we have to fall back on when the dollar is strong and the US is unpredictable?' In short, the driver is a Prabowo government that is simultaneously defending its own position against internal rivals, defending the currency against external pressure, and repositioning Indonesia's trade architecture to reduce dependence on any single partner, all in the same seven-day window.

crystal.eli5:
Indonesia just signed a really big trade deal with Europe after ten years of talking. It covers things like palm oil and medicines, and the government is very proud of it. But signing is only the first step. Next week, everyone will be arguing about who wins and who loses, and the United States will be watching closely because Indonesia is doing this partly to show it does not need to depend on America.

At the same time, the Indonesian money (the rupiah) is getting weaker and weaker against the dollar. The central bank had to raise interest rates in a hurry, which is like turning up the price of borrowing money to try to stop people from selling the rupiah. It helped a little, but experts say the fight is not over. If the rupiah keeps falling, things people buy from other countries, like fuel and food, get more expensive, and that makes life harder for regular families.

There is also a big scandal. It turns out the president's own security team may have been secretly listening to his phone calls. Two senior police officials, including a general, got fired over it, and the government sent soldiers into the capital city, which is a big deal. The story is probably near its peak now, but there may be a few more people named or charged. Meanwhile, the vice-president's seat is still empty, and the politicians are quietly figuring out who gets it before a vote in early December.

The forest fires in Borneo are still going, and the smog is still drifting over into Singapore and Malaysia. The president apologized to his neighbors, then quickly said it was not all Indonesia's fault, which did not go down well. Farmers in the affected areas are getting creative with their protests, like cementing their own feet to the ground to show they are stuck and frustrated. The dry season is not over, so the fires are not going to stop on their own.

A few other things are happening too. Indonesia announced a huge package of partnerships with China worth over seventy billion dollars, which is a big strategic move. The government is also cracking down on big companies in the mining and palm-oil sectors, taking a bigger share of the profits for the state. And Google deleted nineteen thousand YouTube channels that were friendly to the government, which is making the ruling party very angry.

measurement.happened:
This week in Chile was dominated by three interlocking stories: a sharp economic contraction, the political fallout from proposed spending cuts, and a heated international debate over who gets to control Chile's copper and critical minerals.

Economic downturn and central bank maneuvering. The single most consequential headline of the week came from Bloomberg on November 18: Chile's economy suffered its biggest quarterly GDP plunge since 2020. That is a significant event for a country that had been positioning itself as a stable emerging-market economy, and it immediately put pressure on the government's fiscal plans. Around the same time, the central bank was actively managing the financial system: Reuters reported on November 16 that the bank held its capital requirement for banks at 1 percent, and Bloomberg reported on November 17 that the central bank said its new rules had eased the fallout from swap losses. Taken together, these headlines paint a picture of a central bank trying to keep the banking sector stable while the broader economy contracts. The iShares MSCI Chile ETF headline from Reuters on November 15 is a minor data point but reflects the kind of investor attention that a sharp GDP decline attracts. The Transener profile on Bloomberg (November 18) is a smaller item but sits within the same energy-and-infrastructure context.

Protests and clashes over spending cuts. Reuters reported on November 18 that Chileans clashed in Santiago while protesting proposed government spending cuts. This is the direct political consequence of the economic numbers: the government is trying to tighten the belt, and ordinary citizens are hitting the streets. The word 'clashes' suggests this was not a peaceful walk; there was at least some physical confrontation. This is the kind of story that can snowball quickly in a country with a memory of the 2019 social uprising, so the government is likely to feel pressure to respond within days.

The copper and critical-minerals scramble. Three headlines cluster around this theme. First, Reuters on November 20 reported that Chile's Kast (presumably the president or a senior minister) announced boosted cooperation with Japan on critical minerals. Second, Bloomberg on the same day reported that a visit by Bill Gates fueled a public row over who should own Chile's copper, suggesting the Gates visit touched a raw nerve about foreign control of a national resource. Third, Reuters on November 17 reported that Xi urged deeper China-Chile cooperation in AI, polar research, and deep-sea exploration. The pattern is clear: Chile is courted simultaneously by Japan, China, and the United States (via Gates) over its mineral and scientific assets, and the domestic debate about sovereignty over copper is getting louder.

Business and consumer news. The Financial Times reported on November 19 that PriceSmart, the membership warehouse club, began selling memberships in Chile, expanding into its 14th market. This is a sign of continued foreign retail investment in the country and will likely generate consumer-level news in the coming days as the first stores open. The Sociedad Hipodromo Chile stock headline from Reuters on November 17 is a minor corporate-market item.

Sports and miscellany. BBC ran two sports pieces: Chile U17 versus Algeria U17 in the FIFA U17 World Cup (November 20) and a Chile versus Colombia friendly match preview (November 17). The AP headline about 'Santiago Trouet' scoring 16 points in a Mississippi college basketball game (November 18) is almost certainly a name-match false positive rather than a story about Chile the country, but it was tagged under the country name in the collection. The overall sports picture is that Chile's youth national team is competing in the U17 World Cup, which will keep generating match reports through the tournament.

If the government is perceived as too rigid, a second round of demonstrations is probable, and I would assign a real chance that the protest cycle intensifies into the weekend of November 22-23. measurement.happened: This week in Peru was dominated by two major events and a backdrop of climate and economic anxiety. The single biggest story was the completion of Pope Leo XIV's twelve-day South American tour, with Peru serving as the final and most personal stop. The Pope, who served as bishop in Peru before his elevation, returned to his former diocese in the remote Andes, visited the Amazon rainforest, and made stops in Chiclayo, Zaa, and Lima. He condemned the violence enveloping Peru, the killing of Indigenous environmental defenders in the Amazon, and the legacy of African enslavement, calling it 'suffering and humiliation.' In a moment that became global news, a rosary thrown by a well-wisher struck him in the eye during a crowd greeting in Lima; he later publicly forgave the person. He rode in a helicopter cockpit with Peruvian Air Force pilots, visited a home for older residents in a port city, and repeatedly called Peru his 'homeland' and 'second homeland.' Afro-Peruvian singer Susana Baca reflected on singing to the Pope and his historic apology. The visit generated enormous media coverage across every outlet listed, and TV5Monde devoted three French-language pieces to the unusual moments of the trip, from the rosary incident to the helicopter ride. The second major event was a magnitude 6.7 to 6.8 earthquake that struck Peru's Andean region on November 21. Multiple sources (Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) confirmed the quake, noting that Lima residents rushed onto the streets but that no casualties or significant structural damage were immediately reported. The timing, just days after the Pope's visit, gave the event added symbolic weight. Underlying both stories was a thread of climate and economic stress. COP31, the UN climate summit, was running in or around Lima and had stretched past its schedule with no deal in sight; the draft text had omitted fossil fuels, drawing criticism from climate envoys who warned the talks risked failure. US Democrats expressed cautious hope for a climate policy comeback. President Fujimori publicly appealed to China's President Xi for 'goodwill' and financial help to cope with El Niño, a request that underscored Peru's vulnerability to climate extremes. Bloomberg reported that Peru's economy had unexpectedly slowed, with both mining and farming sectors slumping, a pattern consistent with El Niño's impact on agriculture and on mineral extraction. A Bloomberg piece on the 'climate-conscious world devouring beef' also touched Peru's agricultural export base. In short, the week combined a deeply personal and symbolic papal homecoming, a significant seismic event, a stalled global climate negotiation hosted by or involving Peru, and early signs of economic softening tied to weather and commodity cycles.

The president asked China to help pay for the damage that El Niño, a weather pattern that brings too much rain to the north and too little to the south, is doing to the country. And the economy is slowing down — both the mines and the farms are not doing as well as they should. These are not single dramatic events; they are like a slow leak in a tire that you can feel getting flatter every day.

It is a week of looking at the damage and trying to decide what to do next, not a week of new explosions or surprises. Unless the Andes decide to shake again.

This week in Vietnam was dominated by a legislative push on land and development, a visible energy squeeze, and a growing sense of friction in trade and capital markets. Let me walk through it theme by theme.

**Land and development law.** The single biggest story of the week is that Vietnam passed a new law specifically designed to speed up land expropriation for priority projects. Both Reuters (November 21) and Bloomberg (November 21) covered this. The law is aimed at cutting through the notoriously slow process of acquiring land for state-priority infrastructure, industrial zones, and large developer projects. In plain terms, the government is making it legally easier and faster to take private land for public or semi-public use. This is a significant shift in Vietnam's property and investment landscape, where land disputes and protracted negotiations have been a chronic drag on construction and foreign investment. Expect the law to be both celebrated by developers and the state planning apparatus and resented by the families and smallholders who lose plots.

**Energy squeeze and the Russia angle.** Two headlines point to the same underlying stress: Vietnam is running short on power. Bloomberg (November 19) reports that Vietnam has tripled its LNG imports because El Niño has dried up reservoirs and sapped hydropower output, which has historically supplied a large share of the grid. At the same time, Reuters (November 19) reports that Vietnamese and Russian leaders used the APEC summit to agree to deepen energy cooperation, and AP (November 19) notes that Russian nuclear-capable bombers departed Vietnam around the same time Putin was meeting other world leaders in China. The picture is of a country that needs more energy, is looking to Russia as a supplier and partner, and is using the APEC platform to lock in that relationship. The bomber detail is a small but telling signal that the military-diplomatic layer of the Russia-Vietnam relationship is active, even if the bombers were likely in transit or on a goodwill stop.

**EU tariffs on Vietnamese steel.** Reuters (November 16) reports that the EU has set tariffs on steel imports from a group of countries that includes Vietnam alongside India, Japan, Taiwan, and Turkey. For Vietnam, which has been ramping up steel production and exports to capture market share, this is a direct hit on a growing export sector. It also fits a broader pattern of the EU tightening trade protection against what it sees as overcapacity and dumping, particularly from Asian producers. Vietnamese steelmakers will now face higher costs to sell into Europe, and the government may look for retaliatory measures or bilateral talks.

**Airport trouble.** Bloomberg (November 19) reports that Vietnam's new airport has hit yet another snag, with airlines asking for a delay in operations. This is part of a recurring pattern in Vietnamese mega-projects where the opening date keeps slipping. For a country that is building out its aviation capacity to support tourism and trade, repeated delays erode confidence among carriers and passengers and add cost.

**Financial markets: retail investors fleeing stocks for deposits.** Bloomberg (November 15) reports that retail investors in Vietnam are dumping stocks and moving their money into bank deposits that are paying near 10 percent. That is a striking signal. It suggests that the stock market is not delivering enough return to justify the risk, or that deposit rates have been raised sharply (possibly by the central bank to fight inflation or defend the dong), making cash a very attractive alternative. The net effect is a brain drain of retail liquidity out of equities, which puts downward pressure on the VN-Index and on the valuations of listed companies.

**Corporate and legal drama.** Bloomberg (November 16) reports that a celebrity judge from Vietnam's version of Shark Tank has been jailed for money laundering in a case dubbed the 'Mr Pips' fraud. This is a high-visibility case because the person is a TV personality, and the fraud involves what sounds like a forex or investment-scheme scandal. It feeds the public narrative that Vietnam's business-elite and media stars are not above the law, and it may trigger a wave of scrutiny on other celebrity investors and their side ventures.

**Agribusiness and technology.** The Financial Times (November 17) reports that Bunge and CP are expanding a blockchain-enabled soybean traceability collaboration to Vietnam. This is a smaller but interesting story: it signals that Vietnam is being integrated into a global supply-chain transparency push for soy, which matters because Vietnam is a growing soybean processor and exporter. The blockchain angle is more about brand trust and food-safety certification than about the technology itself.

In sum, the week was about Vietnam trying to build faster (land law), power its economy through a tough energy season (LNG, Russia), defend its trade position (EU tariffs), manage its capital markets (retail outflows), and deal with the usual mix of corporate scandal and infrastructure delay that comes with rapid growth.

crystal.headline: Vietnam's land law ignites local disputes as energy crunch and EU tariffs pile pressure
emoji_reasons: The new land-expropriation law is the single biggest story of the week and will drive implementation news, developer reactions, and local smallholder disputes next week.
El Niño has drained hydropower reservoirs, LNG imports are tripled, and the Russia energy deal is in implementation; grid stress and fuel-price adjustments are likely to dominate the news cycle.
The EU has just imposed tariffs on Vietnamese steel and Vietnam will issue a formal reaction, while the US IP probe remains a background overhang extending to February.
crystal.tldr: Vietnam's new land-expropriation law will move from headline to ground-level friction, generating developer celebrations and at least one visible local dispute over the coming week. The energy squeeze from El Niño will persist, with likely grid-stress events and implementation details of the Russia energy deal. The EU steel tariff will draw a formal Vietnamese government or industry response, and the State Bank will face pressure to address the 10-percent deposit rate that is draining retail money out of stocks.
crystal.eli5:
Vietnam just passed a law that makes it easier for the government to take people's land to build big projects like factories and roads. That sounds good for the country's growth, but it means some families are going to be really unhappy, and next week we might see a few small protests or public arguments in the provinces where the land is being taken. Think of it like your school deciding to pave over the playground to build a new gym, and the kids who used to play there are upset.

At the same time, Vietnam is running out of electricity. The rivers that power the dams are dry because of a weather pattern called El Niño, so the country has had to buy a lot more natural gas from other countries, including Russia. Next week, we might see some cities have to turn off the power for a few hours, or the government might raise fuel prices. It's a bit like running a marathon when your water bottle is half empty, and you can't refill it until the next aid station.

On top of that, the European Union just told Vietnam it's going to charge extra fees on steel that Vietnam sells to Europe. Vietnam is going to push back, probably with a statement from its trade ministry or its steel industry group. And because the government has been raising interest rates to keep prices from going too high, regular people are moving their savings out of the stock market and into bank accounts that pay about 10 percent. That means the stock market is getting weaker, and the central bank is in a tough spot: keep rates high to fight inflation, or cut them to help the stock market and the economy grow.

EU tariffs on Vietnamese steel, combined with the broader trade-friction backdrop, make trade and export competitiveness a central economic story of the week.
The El Niño-driven energy squeeze, tripling of LNG imports, and the Russia energy deal all point to power and fuel security as Vietnam's most urgent operational challenge right now.

measurement.happened:
PROTESTS AND COST-OF-LIVING CRISES. The single dominant story of the week in France is the ongoing wave of social mobilization. This was the sixth consecutive Saturday of nationwide marches against the cost of living, public services, and wages. AFP reported more than 100,000 people on the streets, Bloomberg put the figure at 146,000, and unions vowed to keep up the pressure. Reuters and TV5Monde noted that turnout was lower than in earlier weeks and the marches were largely peaceful, though TV5Monde recorded more than 400 arrests and Al Jazeera highlighted student protests at schools. The October 17 riots that preceded this wave cost French insurers 207 million euros according to France Assureurs, as reported by TV5Monde. A Black Bloc group told CNN about using violence as a tool in the protests. France temporarily banned firework mortars amid school protests, and Paris banned gatherings around certain lycées and universities. The overall picture is a society under sustained economic pressure that has not yet found a political solution, with the government under visible strain. Headlines from Reuters, AFP, Bloomberg, CNN, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera, and BBC all support this theme.

PRESIDENTIAL RACE 2027 HEATS UP. The 2027 presidential race is rapidly filling with new entrants and shifting alliances. Former Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin launched his bid on November 20, warning against a Le Pen victory, as reported by Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, and FT. Judo champion Teddy Riner shocked the political world with a surprise candidacy announced on November 15, per BBC. The Green party's leader offered to support hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, boosting his chances, according to Reuters. The Justice minister publicly said Mélenchon could win the election, which Reuters reported. A poll showed Le Pen and Mélenchon ahead, per Reuters. Le Pen promised to lower the retirement age to as low as 60 and to add private savings to the pension system, reported by FT and Bloomberg. Centrist candidate Philippe pledged radical reforms to avoid a financial crisis, per Reuters. Bloomberg noted that attacks on France's political elite are making Mélenchon a wild card, and the Financial Times observed that France's once best hope of stopping Le Pen is losing ground. The Wall Street Journal ran an essay on the political taboo tearing France apart. This is a crowded, fragmented field with no clear anti-Le Pen consensus forming.

POLICE RACISM VERDICT AND JUSTICE SCANDALS. A landmark ruling saw three French police officers sentenced to prison for the racist assault on Black music producer Michel Zecler, as reported by Reuters, AP, CNN, Al Jazeera, and BBC. This is being called a watershed moment in French police accountability. Simultaneously, veteran actor Gérard Depardieu and author Michel Houellebecq were placed under investigation for sexual assault, per Reuters, BBC, and AFP. Depardieu withdrew his appeal against an earlier conviction and apologized to victims, reported by Reuters and AFP. The first masculinism trial in France saw about thirty men accused of misogynist and racist remarks, per TV5Monde. Parents were jailed for the torture and death of a four-year-old girl nearly forty years earlier, per BBC. These stories collectively paint a picture of a justice system confronting long-buried institutional and social failures.

BUDGET, DEBT, AND ECONOMIC TENSION. France's fiscal position remains a source of domestic and European anxiety. The EU Commission said France will miss its deficit targets as economic growth falters, per Bloomberg, and flagged France as having the weakest outlook in the euro zone, per Reuters. The French presidency called the latest EU budget proposal very disappointing, per Reuters. The Bank of France governor, in a CNBC exclusive interview, said bond spreads are too high amid market overreaction but acknowledged the deficit and debt are too high to ignore, and that he does not see a recession despite strikes and uncertainty. The ECB said markets should help discipline France over its high debt, per Reuters. Bloomberg's analysis asked what France can do to break its budget deadlock. Le Pen's proposal to tap private savings for pensions, reported by FT and Bloomberg, signals how the fiscal crisis is becoming a campaign issue.

UKRAINE AND FOREIGN POLICY. France is stepping up its involvement in the Ukraine conflict while carefully managing its rhetoric. France sought a UN Security Council meeting after strikes on Kyiv, per Reuters. A French minister insisted France is not a co-belligerent in Ukraine, per Reuters. Macron said Ukraine's NATO membership is relevant for European security, per Reuters. The AP detailed how France is sending soldiers into Ukraine for a training mission called Volia, and how Russia is responding. TV5Monde explained the Volia mission. France and the UK will host a December conference on the Russian shadow fleet, per Reuters. Macron denounced Russia's aggressive agenda on European territory as an irresponsible bet, per TV5Monde. Le Pen said France will keep giving Ukraine aid even if she is elected, per Reuters. France also deepened ties with Cambodia (29 agreements, a restored temple inaugurated by Macron), Malaysia (rare earths and strategic partnership), and Morocco (accelerated bilateral cooperation), per TV5Monde, Reuters, and Bloomberg.

ECB SUCCESSION AND EUROPEAN INSTITUTIONS. France and Germany secured key roles at the ECB, with France's Moulin expected in a senior position and Spain set for the presidency, per Reuters and FT. The FT detailed how Paris and Berlin sealed the ECB succession. This is a significant diplomatic win for France in European economic governance.

FOOTBALL AND SPORTS. French football chief Philippe Diallo formally announced his challenge to Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency, backed by UEFA and the German FA, as reported by Reuters, AP, AFP, DW, FT, and Al Jazeera. In club and national team football, France beat Turkey 2-1 to qualify top in a group, per TV5Monde. The Nations League quarterfinal draw paired France with Spain, per multiple sources. In rugby, fly-half Matthieu Jalibert returned to the France squad ahead of a clash with Argentina, per AFP and TV5Monde. In tennis, France's Arthur Fils was eliminated at the ATP Finals, per AFP. Chelsea beat Paris Saint-Germain 1-0 in the Women's Champions League, per BBC. Bordeaux made headlines with a bid to return from the amateur sixth tier, per BBC.

NUCLEAR AND ENERGY. EDF is close to finalizing a roughly 14 billion euro nuclear construction deal for new reactors, per Reuters and Bloomberg. Engie's chief rejected Mélenchon's call for nationalization, per Reuters. RTE said there is no particular vigilance needed for electricity supply this winter, per TV5Monde. This signals France's continued commitment to nuclear energy as a strategic pillar.

POLICE SHOOTINGS LAW AND GOVERNMENT POLITICS. The French Senate approved a police shootings law that critics dub a licence to kill, per Reuters. The Interior Minister summoned an official allegedly leaked confidential information to the far-right RN, and France formally questioned that official, per Reuters and AP. Macron fustigated a discourse of jealousy and hate of success, and said he did his best despite errors, per TV5Monde. These internal government tensions show a cabinet under pressure from both the street and the opposition.

HEALTH, SCIENCE, AND ENVIRONMENT. France is on high alert for bird flu as a seasonal wave spreads, per Reuters. The European Court of Human Rights validated France's mandatory vaccination for healthcare workers, per TV5Monde. Antibiotic use is slightly down but bacterial resistance is rising, per TV5Monde. A French advocate for banning forever chemicals dreamed of a worldwide ban, per AFP. COP31: France hopes for a compromise on the IPCC question, per TV5Monde.

BUSINESS AND TECHNOLOGY. OVHcloud launched AI cloud products hosted in Europe, per Reuters. Vusion launched a 97 million dollar bid for Swedish peer Pricer, per Reuters. The Agnelli family doubled its stake in French diagnostics company BioMérieux, per FT. Milbank swooped on Weil's Paris office, per FT. Cdiscount offered preferential conditions to Made in France companies, per TV5Monde. Apple faces a French trial over alleged planned obsolescence of iPhones, per AFP. France and Malaysia deepened their strategic partnership on rare earths, defense, and hybrid threats, per TV5Monde and Bloomberg.
